3 
Climate Leadership and Community Protection Act
4 
Q.
Given that the CLCPA is a new policy issue not addressed in previous cases, please
5 
comment on its relevance.
6 
A.
The CLCPA, in conjunction with additional proposed legislation in the Governor’s
7 
budget, is intended to reduce and then eliminate greenhouse gas emissions in New
8 
York State.  Over time, this legislation will reduce gas use, revenue and access to
9 
external capital.  It is critical that new mandated capital expenditures be financed with
10 
internally generated funds (principally depreciation) and that depreciable lives match
11 
the expected economic lives of utility assets.  The Company believes that either
12 
systematic replacement capital expenditures have to be curtailed or the depreciable
13 
lives of assets have to be reduced.  It is imperative that depreciable lives are reconciled
14 
with the expectations of the CLCPA in this case, rather than delaying such action.
15 
First, nominal gas commodity prices are low, so consumer impacts will be mitigated.
16 
Second, it is important to stabilize/reduce rate base while the Company’s customer
17 
count remains high.  Third, it is confiscatory to mandate large capital expenditures and
18 
not provide depreciable lives consistent with CLCPA.
19 
As the CLCPA takes effect, volumes will be reduced and rate base should decline in
20 
parallel.  Addressing the CLCPA and depreciation in this case is consistent with how
21 
the Commission addressed the federal Tax Cuts and Jobs Act of 2017 (the "Federal
22 
Tax Act") in Case 17-M-0815 (i.e., generic proceedings for companies not before the
23 
PSC in a rate case; individual rate cases for companies already before the Commission
24 
51


--- Page 52 ---
4834-7495-4933.8 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF FIROUZEH SARHANGI 
FS-6 
in a rate case).  The reasoning applied by the Commission in the Federal Tax Act 
1 
context is applicable here to consideration of the impact of the CLCPA. 
2 
Q.
Have you reflected the impact of the CLCPA in the Company’s revenue
3 
requirement?
4 
A.
Yes.  New York State passed the CLCPA that mandates reduced greenhouse gas
5 
emissions to 60% of 1990 levels by 2030, and 15% of 1990 levels by 2050, with the
6 
remaining emission reduction achieved by controlled offsets.  The CLCPA also
7 
requires electric generators to meet 70% of demand with renewable energy by 2030.
8 
These climate change and greenhouse gas initiatives will impact the Company's
9 
customer base over time.  The initiatives will also increase the Company’s cost of
10 
environmental compliance by increasing reporting requirements and requiring the
11 
Company to repair all leaks and replace all leak prone pipe.  This will adversely
12 
affect the Company’s ability to raise funds.  The CLCPA has a very direct and
13 
undeniable impact on Corning's facilities and construction expenditures.  In addition
14 
to requiring greater expenditures to address the CLCPA's mandates, the new law
15 
effectively shortens the effective life of the Company's existing and future
16 
investment in infrastructure.  As a consequence of these impacts of the CLCPA, we
17 
are proposing that the service lives of the Company's fixed assets be reduced to 30
18 
years for purposes of calculating depreciation expense.
19 
Adequate depreciation will allow the Company to continue it systematic
20 
replacement program with more internally generated funds.  Given the CLCPA
21 
external funds will become increasingly difficult to generate at competitive rates,
22 
even though the Commission continues to require significant investment in pipe
23 
replacement and other system upgrades.  It is confiscatory to base rates on
24 
52


--- Page 53 ---
4834-7495-4933.8 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF FIROUZEH SARHANGI 
FS-7 
depreciable lives of 60 years when those investments have an effective life of 30 
1 
years or less. 
2 
Q.
Has the Company completed a study that measures the impact on average service
3 
lives?
4 
A 
Yes.  Mr. Paul Normand of Management Applications Consulting, Inc. ("MAC")
5 
discusses the results of that study in his testimony.
6 
Q.
What is the impact of the CLCPA on the revenue requirement?
7 
A.

8 
CLCPA will require an accelerated schedule for recovery of depreciation expense.
9 
Consequently, depreciation expense will increase $3,065,97 over the amount
10 
currently in rates ($2,021,432).  This represents approximately one-half of the
11 
requested Rate Year one rate increase.
12 
Q 
The CLCPA calls for a multi-year study period for development of an
13 
implementation plan does it not?
14 
A.
Yes.
15 
Q.

Productivity Imputation and Inflation Allowance
12 
Q.
Can you provide historical perspective on the Commission’s application of the
13 
productivity imputation?
14 
A.
Yes.  In the recent past, a productivity adjustment of at least 1% has been applied
15 
virtually automatically in rate cases in New York.  Indeed, in the 2009 Rate Order in
16 
Case 08-G-1137, the Commission adopted a productivity adjustment of 2%.  In the
17 
April 20, 2012 Order Adopting Terms of Joint Proposal and Establishing a Multi-Year
18 
Rate Plan (the “2012 Rate Order”) in Case 11-G-0280, the Commission adopted an
19 
adjustment of 1%.  Originally, the Commission would apply such an adjustment in the
20 
absence of a clear demonstration that there was at least 1% productivity already
21 
included in the historical test year that would continue through the rate year.
22 
Q.
Do you believe that the 1% or 2 % productivity adjustment is warranted in this case?
23 
62


--- Page 63 ---
4834-7495-4933.8 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF FIROUZEH SARHANGI 
FS-17 
A.
No.  The Commission’s October 18, 2007 Order in an Orange and Rockland Utilities,
1 
Inc. rate proceeding (Cases 06-E-1433, 06-E-1547), stated that the productivity
2 
adjustment “is a surrogate for specific adjustments to overall productivity gains”
3 
(p. 19).  If productivity is achieved by a utility, there is no justification for applying
4 
the “surrogate.”  Corning has clearly increased its productivity by reducing costs, as
5 
discussed below.  Such control and avoidance of costs demonstrates that at least the
6 
equivalent of a 2% productivity adjustment is already embedded in customer rates and,
7 
therefore, no further productivity adjustment is necessary or appropriate.
8

9

10 
transporting locally produced natural gas from the wellhead into the Company’s
11

12 
derived from this effort has resulted in revenue pass back to customers of
13 
approximately $6.2 million.  In addition to their share of transportation revenues,
14 
customers are benefitting from lower overall gas costs because locally produced gas
15 
requires less transportation than traditional supplies from the Gulf Coast and other
16 
distant sources.  Corning consistently has some of the lowest cost gas in the State.
17 
Over both the near and the long term, therefore, Corning’s customers stand to benefit
18 
substantially from the Company’s innovation and creativity.
19 
Corning has actively pursued expansion of the Company’s customer base.  Such
20 
expansion not only provides needed service to the “new” customers, but also helps to
21 
spread the Company’s fixed costs over a broader base, bringing down those costs to all
22 
customers.  As with construction of pipelines and compressor stations to transport
23 
locally produced gas, such expansion of the system in new service territories is not
24 
63


--- Page 64 ---
4834-7495-4933.8

something Corning is required to do in order to meet its public service obligations; it

4

5 
Q.
Are there additional productivity adjustments made by the Commission in rate cases?
6 
A.
Yes.  Although the Commission typically addresses health insurance cost increases in
7 
the context of the inflation allowance, as a practical matter, the manner in which
8 
health insurance costs have been treated nonetheless constitutes an additional
9 
productivity adjustment.
10 
Q.
Please explain.
11 
A.
The Commission’s practice is to include health insurance in the general inflation pool.
12 
While this practice may have been justified in the distant past when health cost
13 
increases were more closely aligned with other cost increases, those days are long
14 
gone.  Unfortunately, health insurance costs continue to outpace inflation by a
15 
substantial margin.  The Commission’s practice, and Staff’s adherence to it, has
16 
unfortunately become a convenient “methodology” that guarantees that Corning and
17 
other utilities will never recover the full cost of health insurance.  I recommend that
18 
the Commission abandon this approach.  Objectively, it has become untenable and
19 
warrants re-examination based on current circumstances.  It should be noted that
20 
Corning goes out to bid for health insurance every year, Corning has increased the
21 
premium paid by employees and taken other actions to limit the increase in health care
22 
costs.
23 
65


--- Page 66 ---
4834-7495-4933.8 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF FIROUZEH SARHANGI 
FS-20 
Q.
What conditions lead you to question the Commission’s typical treatment of health 
1 
care cost increases?
2 
A.
The dominant condition is the difference for Corning between the general inflation
3 
rate and the medical inflation rate (a differential of 5.67X).  The cumulative general
4 
inflation rate is 5.70%, while the cumulative medical inflation rate is projected to be
5 
32.35% from the historical test period to the first Rate Year.
6 
Q.
Have you performed calculations specific to Corning on this issue?
7 
A.
Yes.  Exhibit CNG-9, Schedule 2, presents my analysis.
8 
Q.
What does the analysis show?
9 
A.
The analysis shows that, in order for Corning to recover its projected health care cost
10 
it must experience significant cost decreases in all other items in the inflation pool.
11 
This conclusion flows principally from (a) the fact that health care costs constitute a
12 
significant proportion of the inflation pool (20% of the total); and (b) the rate
13 
differential of 5.67X, as discussed above.  As a consequence, the other items included
14 
in the general inflation allowance of $130,792 (i.e., excluding medical) would have to
15 
decrease by $159,373, or 121% less than the projected amount, to offset the medical
16 
cost increases.
17 
Q.
What do you conclude from the analysis presented in Exhibit CNG-9, Schedule 2?
18 
A.
The notion, assumed in the current Commission practice, that Corning’s health care
19 
cost can be offset by “managing” the rest of the inflation pool expenses, i.e., by
20 
bringing about cost decreases in other items in the general pool, is not sustainable.
21 
The effect of continuing this myth is an imputation of additional “productivity” that
22 
knows no rational basis and could be considered confiscatory by not providing for
23 
recovery of legitimate operating costs.
24

Revenue Requirements 
5 
Q.
What gas revenue increase is Corning seeking in this filing?
6 
A.
As detailed in the Company’s presentation, Corning’s cost of service substantiates an
7 
increase in gas revenues of $6,256,926, $845,142 and $680,913 for the twelve months
8 
ended January 31, 2022, 2023 and 2024, respectively.  The Company is proposing to
9 
levelize the three-year revenue requirement to $3,5234,68.
10 
Q.
What are the principal reasons for the rate increase?
11 
A.
There are several important factors that are driving the need for the proposed increase
12 
in revenue.  As previously discussed, the impact of the CLCPA and cost increases
13 
related to Commission-mandated investments in infrastructure (and the resultant
14 
higher property taxes, depreciation expense and return on capital) to improve the gas
15 
system are the principal drivers.  Cyber security and safety has become a major issue
16 
for utilities.  Therefore, there is a requested increase in personnel and contractors to
17 
handle cyber and safety issues.  These cost increases have been offset to some extent
18 
with revenues from higher sales and additional customer attachments.
19 
Q.
Are there rate moderators that can be used to ameliorate the projected increases?
20 
A.
As previously discussed, the Company believes that the rate increases should be
21 
levelized over the three-year rate plan.  In addition, delaying the decrease in rates
22 
scheduled for June 2020 would allow those amounts to reduce the incremental revenue
23 
71


--- Page 72 ---
4834-7495-4933.8 
DIRECT TESTIMONY OF FIROUZEH SARHANGI 
FS-26 
requirements.  Toward that end, the Company will file a request with the Commission 
1 
to delay the rate decrease. 
2 
Q.
Why is it prudent to delay the rate decrease scheduled for June 2020?
3 
A.
Rates in this case will become effective on February 1, 2021.  If the timing of the rate
4 
decrease is not modified, customers will not see any material impact on their bills for
5 
the non-heating period (June to September) from the June 2020 decrease.  They will
6 
experience a noticeable decrease during the heating season (October 2020 to January
7 
2021), only to experience a jump in rates in February 2021.  The Commission has
8 
consistently tried to minimize volatility in rates and we believe that our proposal to
9 
delay the decrease until the rates set pursuant to this filing become effective is
10 
consistent with that goal.
11 
Q.
How will the rate decrease from June 2020 to January 2021 captured for the benefit of
12 
the customers?
13 
A.
The Company will defer the customer benefit for that period and it will be passed back
14 
to the customer.

Pensions and OPEBS 
3 
Q. 
Please briefly describe the Company’s Pension Plan. 
4 
A. 
The Company has defined benefit pension plans covering all of its employees.  The 
5 
benefits are based on years of service and the employee’s highest average 
6 
compensation during a specified period.  The Company makes annual contributions to 
7 
the plans equal to amounts determined in accordance with the funding requirements of 
8 
the Employee Retirement Income Security Act of 1974 as determined by the 
9 
Company’s actuarial consultant.  The Company follows the accounting requirements 
10 
as prescribed by the Commission in Case 91-M–0890. 
11 
Q. 
Please describe the Company’s post-retirement benefit plan. 
12 
A. 
The Company offers post-retirement benefits comprised of medical and life insurance 
13 
coverage to its employees who meet certain age and service criteria.  Currently, the 
14 
retirees from age 62 to 65 pay 60 percent of their health care premiums until Medicare 
15 
benefits commence at age 65.  After age 65, Medicare supplemental coverage is 
16 
offered with the Company contributing $150 per month toward the cost of the 
17 
insurance.  In a few instances, for employees who retired before a certain date, the 
18 
Company pays for the entire cost of the premium.  In addition, the Company offers 
19 
limited life insurance coverage to retirees.  The post-retirement benefit plan is not 
20 
funded.  The Company follows the accounting requirements prescribed in 
21 
Case 91-M-0890.

Q. 
What is the purpose of your additional direct testimony? 
A. 
Consistent with the Ruling on Procedure and Schedule issued in this proceeding on 
April 24, 2020, as amended by the Ruling Amending Schedule issued on May 11, 
2020, I am providing corrections and updates to the Company's initial filing. 
Q. 
Are you distinguishing between corrections and updates? 
A. 
Yes. 
Q. 
Please explain. 
A. 
I use the term "correction" to refer to material that was incorrect as presented in the 
original filing on February 27, 2020. That material may be incorrect because it 
contains the wrong data, was calculated erroneously, or was improperly labeled or 
formatted in the initial filing. As a related matter, I have identified some items that 
require "reclassification" in the form of transfer or reallocation to different categories 
or accounts. In contrast, I use the term "update" to refer to situations where the 
original presentation was correct at the time of the filing, but where more current data 
are now available and can be appropriately substituted for the original information. 
Also included in the category of "updates" are changes to the Company's original 
position on policies or other issues. In referring to corrections, reclassifications and 
updates collectively or without distinguishing among them, I may use the term 
"changes" or "modifications."

Q. 
Are there any additional matters that you believe should be addressed at this time? 
A. 
Yes. The COVID-19 pandemic affecting our nation and in particular New York State 
will have economic and financial impacts on the Company's operations. 
Q. 
Please explain the economic and fmancial impacts that COVID-19 pandemic will have 
on Company operations 
A. 
The COVID-19 pandemic is having a devastating impact on the local economy in 
Corning's service territory. The Company has already experienced loss of gas load 
and believes that it will experience significantly lower revenues primarily from the 
commercial and industrial sectors. In addition, cash flow will be impacted with higher 
levels of unemployment, cash receipts will decrease and arrears and uncollectible 
accounts will increase. Operationally, customer service and field maintenance and 
construction activities will be impacted. 
Q. 
Can you describe specific operational impacts? 
A. 
Yes. In the customer service area, the lack of access to customer premises during this 
crisis has limited the reading of meters located in a customer's home. The termination 
for non-payment rules have been suspended during this crisis, thereby making 
collection for non-payment difficult. The interaction between customers and the 
Company has been limited because of the social distancing rules, as well as lock-down 
requirements, imposed by New York State. In the field services area, we continue to 
provide a high level of service in emergency response, leak detection and repair. 
However, the maintenance and construction activities related to Commission 
mandated programs such as bare steel replacement have been impacted. 
Q. 
What actions has the Company taken to deal with this crisis?

A.

employees. The Company can respond to any emergency during this period. The 
Company has delayed construction expenditures and operation and maintenance 
expenses are being monitored closely. The Company has asked for waivers on certain 
Commission-mandated programs. The Company has requested a four-month 
extension for its Service Survey Inspection ("SSI") completion date. SSI is the PSC-
mandated program for corrosion and leak inspection of exposed service piping. The 
Company also requested a six-month extension to requirements for replacing leak-
prone pipe (and the related regulatory liability of 8 basis points). Corning cannot 
retire leak-prone pipe without interrupting service to customers. Interruption of service 
requires Corning or its contractor employees to enter customer buildings to make final 
connections and restore service. As previously mentioned, meter reading continues, 
except for meters inside customers' homes. The customer service center is currently 
closed to the public. Customers can make payments via mail, debit/credit cards, bank 
electronic payment or drop box deposit located outside the service center. The 
Customer Service Department is staffed to handle all customer calls and inquiries

payments) will adversely impact the Company's ability to raise capital on favorable 
terms when needed.

It is not cost effective for a company the size of Corning to commission a compensation
4 
study at the expense of investing in infrastructure improvement.  While the Staff witness
5 
relies heavily on the Commission’s 2011 order in Case 10-E-0362, I would note that
6 
allowing incentive compensation in rates has been permitted for at least the last eight years.
7 
The initial requirement to benchmark total compensation was to ensure that utility
8 
compensation was comparable to compensation for similar positions in its service area.
9 
Since the Commission has allowed incentive compensation in rates for larger New York
10 
utilities, it is not cost effective to require a small utility company to spend money on a
11 
compensation study. In order for Corning Natural Gas to be competitive in the New York
12 
employment space, we need to offer current and prospective employees a decent incentive
13 
compensation package and the costs associated with this package should be included in our
14 
revenue requirement.
15 
Q.
Why is the financial performance goal (net income) important and necessary?
16 
A.
Corning’s history of financial weakness and near bankruptcy in 2005 clearly demonstrates
17 
that attention to financial strength and solvency is important to customers, as well as
18 
shareholders.  The achievement of earnings targets enhances the Company’s ability to
19 
access capital markets to fund the purchase of gas supply and to comply with infrastructure
20 
mandates from the Commission.  The achievement of the net income financial goal benefits
21 
both the customers and shareholders.  Staff suggests that the mere existence of that goal is
22 
in conflict with safety and reliability goals.  It is not. In our industry, safety and reliability
23

8

13 
from the nearest station in the Corning area.  As stated above, during the critical months of 
14

15 
in February, there were two days when the average temperature was five below or colder, 
16

17 
were below normal average temperatures.  In addition to these colder-than-normal 
18 
temperatures, the amount of snow cover was an important factor.  The Southern Tier had 
19 
little snow cover for a good portion of the early part of the winter season.  Low or no snow 
20 
cover often leads to deeper levels of frost since the ground is not insulated from the cold air 
21 
by snow cover.  We experienced frost at depths and temperatures that we had not 
22 
experienced in a long time.  We were unable to provide documentation at the time of the

Q. 
Please address the concerns raised by the Staff Panel regarding fund management. 
A. 
In 2019, interest rates declined significantly, which impacts the net present value of 
Corning's pension liability which then produces an actuarial loss in the plan. This 
phenomenon is not unique to Corning. Virtually every well managed pension fund relies 
on interest-bearing obligations to some extent to balance its portfolio of assets in order to 
minimize risk and maximize returns to the plan. In periods of sharply declining interest 
rates, pension plans will experience short term actuarial losses in the plan. See "Exhibit A" 
for a graph depicting the decline in interest rates on U.S. Corporate debt instruments during 
fiscal 2019. With regard to the Staff Panel's concerns regarding the 7.5% expected long-
term rate of return on plan assets, "Exhibit B" shows the fiscal year 2019 performance and 
"Exhibit D" details return performance over a 1-10 year period. Given the performance 
shown on "Exhibit D," the Company remains comfortable that the fund manager has the 
ability to achieve a 7.5% expected return over a full market cycle. The fund's long-term 
performance has been above benchmark with the total, all-in fee being well below the 
average of other plans of comparable size. The fund fees are detailed in "Exhibit E." In 
response to Staff's request for information on the pension plan's investment policies, please 
refer to "Exhibit C," which is the Company's Investment Policy Statement. Please note that 
the Company does not pre-fund its OPEB liability, so the Company maintains no assets in a 
fund from which OPEB liabilities are paid. The Company believes that it has adequate 
controls and review procedures over its investment manager. In 2007, the Company

A. 
Not entirely. I agree that identification and pursuit of RNG supplies is within the purview 
of the gas supply group and is unlikely to result in any significant incremental expense. On 
the other hand, there are at least two types of costs that are incremental and that should be 
recovered: (a) the capital expenditure associated building a new RNG interconnect or 
upgrading existing facilities to allow for an RNG interconnect, and (b) the commodity cost 
associated with RNG supply. The capital cost component should be recovered via a 
surcharge mechanism for each applicable service class. The RNG commodity cost, 
whether local or upstream, should be recovered via the existing Gas Adjustment Clause 
mechanism in the same manner as other commodity costs. 
Q. 
At page 14 of his testimony, Mr. Riebel recommends that "the Company incorporate a plan 
to include NPAs as an alternative to traditional gas infrastructure investment since it may 
be a few years until they file for rates again." Do you concur with that recommendation? 
A. 
Generally, yes. The implementation approach described by Mr. Riebel appears reasonable. 
The Company believes, however, that it is important to clarify that acceptable NPAs may 
include both Demand-Side Solutions ("DSS") and Supply-Side Solutions ("SSS"). DSM 
can be further categorized as targeted demand response, targeted energy efficiency, heat 
pumps, thermal storage, other electrification and fuel switching, and behavior change and 
market transformation. SSS typically consist of alternate supply delivery methods such as 
on-system RNG supply, on-system liquefied natural gas ("LNG") peaking storage, 
compressed and LNG trucking (virtual pipelines) and LNG liquefaction port terminals.

21

22

23 
Corning can do very little to change or improve.  Per Case 16-G-0369, Corning is 
24 
232


--- Page 233 ---

Q. 
In its testimony, Staff discusses the leaks existing on piping traversing the flood 
control lands in the Corning area. Does Corning agree with Staff's proposal? 
A. 
Corning agrees that the leaks should be addressed through our leak prone pipe 
replacement program and has maintained that as our position since originally 
approached by the DEC. Many of these Type 3 leaks are in areas where we may not 
be allowed to perform direct replacement (i.e. new pipe placed parallel and adjacent to 
the existing pipe) but instead will be forced to place the new pipe onto municipal or 
private property. Doing so likely requires longer lengths of pipe and far greater 
expense than if we were able to install the new facility adjacent to the existing one. 
We have informed the DEC that any one of these projects would be a significant 
portion of our annual capital budget and as a result we may perform only one of these 
projects per year. Therefore, the leak repairs on flood control lands may take several 
years to complete. Corning has been and will continue to work with the DEC on these 
leak repairs. Corning appreciates being allowed to count the entire length of pipe 
installed on these leak repair installations within the flood control lands towards the 
annual leak prone pipe target. Corning also agrees to maintain records of the length of 
main replaced within these flood control areas. We understand that we will be 
allowed to defer the incremental cost of the installation over $33.96 per foot but no

EMERGENCY RESPONSE 
Q 
Does Corning agree with Staffs proposal to increase the negative revenue adjustments 
(NRA) from six, four and two basis points to twelve, eight and five basis points for 
failure to meet the 30, 45, and sixty minute targets, respectively? 
A. 
Staff states that it is reasonable to increase these NRAs to incentivize Corning to avoid 
backsliding from its current performance. Corning disagrees with Staff's position that 
the NRAs should be increased and with the justification for the increase, i.e., as an 
incentive to prevent our backsliding. Corning wishes to maintain the NRAs at their 
current levels of six, four, and two basis points. Staff stated in its testimony (page 30, 
line 23) that historical data shows that Corning has constantly met the targets for this 
metric. We have shown no evidence of backsliding or missing our Emergency 
Response targets in the past. We are already incentivized to meet our targets and have 
done so. We believe penalizing us for consistently meeting a target is inappropriate.

Corning believes that this level of exposure is unfair. Given our size, a small change 
in the number of total damages has a large effect on our rate. As an example, if we are 
issued 4,700 tickets per year and our total damages are eight, we would have a rate of 
1.70. Only four additional damages that year would jump our rate to 2.55. Corning 
would like to reduce the NRA for the 2.50 or greater rate from twenty basis points to 
fifteen basis points.

THE 1.1 MILES OF PIPE LOCATED AT SULLWAN PARK SCIENCE CENTER 
Q. 
The Panel makes several recommendations regarding the pipe located within the 
Sullivan Park facility that Corning recently acquired, including the filing of a report 
within 60 days of the filing date of Staff's direct testimony (i.e., by August 25, 2020). 
Please discuss Corning's response to these recommendations. 
A. 
Corning understands the importance of assuring the integrity of this natural gas system 
and will do what it must to achieve this objective. We have begun the necessary 
O&M work to assimilate this segment of pipe into our system. To date we have 
performed a leak survey over the entire system including bar holes in the ground at the 
service line entrance. We have initiated a complete locate and mark-out process in 
cooperation with Corning Incorporated of the 1.1 miles of pipe. This system will have 
CP readings taken and remediation as needed, this summer. The below-ground valves 
will be excavated by Corning Incorporated this summer/fall to assure operability. The 
basic system map provided by Corning Incorporated has been transferred to Corning 
Natural Gas' mapping. The mapping will be updated as system locating progresses.

MONTHLY LEAK REPORT 
Q. 
Pursuant to Case 05-G-1539, Corning has been required to submit a monthly Leak 
Repair Status Report to the Secretary. This report contains system leak survey status, 
quantity of leaks discovered, quantity of leaks repaired, and quantity of main and 
services replaced since last report. Although Staff did not address the subject of the 
monthly leak report in its testimony, do you have any recommendation regarding this 
report? 
A. 
Yes. Corning would like to discontinue sending this report to the Department of 
Public Service. This report was required by Safety Staff during a time in the 
Company's history when system maintenance and leak repairs were minimal and the 
number of leaks in the Corning system were much greater. None of these conditions 
exist today. Since the time this report was first required we have replaced more than 
60% of our leak prone pipe and almost 40% of our leak prone services, and we have 
repaired over 3,700 leaks. With the Company's current leak repair trajectory and 
facility replacement program, we will soon be maintaining a small to non-existent leak 
backlog. Accordingly, this report has become obsolete and should be discontinued.

WEATHER NORMALIZATION 
15 
Q.
What is the purpose of a weather normalization adjustment? 
16 
A.
For the purposes of cost of service studies and rate making, the test year must represent 
17 
typical or normal circumstances.  The Company has identified specific pro forma 
18 
adjustments to the test year to reflect the expenses that normally would be anticipated in 
19 
the test year, based on those changes which are known and measurable at the present 
20 
time.  However, another important adjustment is the Company’s CCF sales which are 
21 
weather sensitive.  Even small variations in weather can have a material impact on the 
22 
sales and related revenues, especially for a gas utility.  The weather normalization 
23 
276


--- Page 277 ---
4818-8882-3989.2 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 6 of 22 
adjustment is targeted to identify the change in sales and revenue that would have been 
1 
anticipated if the actual weather in the test year had been exactly normal.  The use of 
2 
these adjustments in the allocation process provides a more robust cost of service result 
3 
which can then be used as a reasonable foundation for the Company’s proposed rate 
4 
design. 
5

ACCOUNTING COST OF SERVICE STUDY 
1 
Allocated Cost of Service Study 
2 
Q. 
Would you briefly define an Allocated Cost of Service Study?
3 
A. 
The cost to serve the customers of any utility company consists generally of operating 
4 
expenses and return.  For a historical test period, these costs are on record and the overall 
5 
cost to serve the collective customers of the utility may be readily established.  On the 
6 
other hand, the unique cost to serve customers of the various service classifications is 
7 
much less apparent.  Costs can vary significantly between customer classes depending 
8 
upon the nature of their demands upon the system and the facilities required to serve 
9 
them.  The purpose of an Allocated Cost of Service Study is to assign or allocate each 
10 
relevant component of cost on an appropriate basis in order to determine the proper cost 
11 
to serve.  The result is a cost matrix displaying for each cost category the detailed costs 
12 
of serving each customer class in this study. 
13 
14 
Q. 
Please describe the procedure that you used in preparing your Allocated Cost of 
15 
Service Study?
16 
A. 
Through the application of a computerized microcomputer cost model developed by 
17 
Management Applications Consulting specifically for Corning Natural Gas Corporation's 
18 
operations, it was possible to treat each element of Rate Base, Revenue and Operating 
19 
Expense in detail and to assign or allocate each item to the customer classes.  The 
20 
complete detailed allocation process is presented in Schedule PMN-6.  Specific pro 
21 
forma adjustments to this test year are discussed in detail in the Company’s testimony 
22 
279


--- Page 280 ---
4818-8882-3989.2 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 9 of 22 
and have been identified in the detailed cost of service study presented in 
1 
Schedule PMN-6.

on the adjusted historical test year ended September 30, 2019.  The detailed cost of 
9 
service study which supports Schedule PMN-4 is provided in Schedule PMN-6).

Description of Cost Model 
12 
Q. 
How does the computerized cost model operate?
13 
A.
The cost model is essentially a cost matrix.  The vertical dimension of the study consists 
14 
of the costs to serve as provided by the Company.  The development of the cost of 
15 
service study begins with rate base and continues with revenues, operating expenses, 
16 
taxes, and the computation of a labor allocator. The cost model includes three additional 
17 
pieces, a summary of costs to serve, a list of the allocation factors employed in the study 
18 
and a revenue requirements section.  The horizontal portion consists of the assignment of 
19 
all costs to each of the Company’s customer classes. 
20 
21 
Each page, starting with page 1 has an important column immediately preceding the 
22 
numerical data marked “ALLOC”, an abbreviation for ALLOCATOR.  The ALLOC 
23 
column contains an acronym to indicate the allocation factor used to allocate the costs

shown in the Total Company Column to each customer class.  A tabulation of these

been provided at the end of the study beginning on page 41 in Schedule PMN-6. 
3 
4 
Using these allocation factors, costs shown in the Total Company column that were not

Q. 
Mr. Normand, please describe the allocation of Distribution Mains Acct 376 to
16 
customer classes. 
17 
A.
The Distribution Mains account has been classified as demand (34.75%) and customer 
18 
(65.25%) related based on the results of the minimum-size study described below.  The 
19 
Distribution Mains account was separated into two cost categories: 2-inch and below and 
20 
above 2 inches.  The 2-inch and below account for 47.2% of Distribution Mains and are 
21 
classified as customer related.  Since most large customers are not served by a 2-inch or 
22 
smaller sized pipe, this customer related portion, 30.80% (65.25%*47.2%), is allocated 
23 
to the Residential and Small Commercial rate classes based on their respective customer 
24 
282


--- Page 283 ---
4818-8882-3989.2 
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 12 of 22 
counts.  The remaining customer related portion of mains greater than 2 inches, 34.45% 
1 
(65.25*(100.0% - 47.2%)), is allocated on an adjusted customer allocation factor.   
2 
3 
The adjusted customer allocation factor approach is to fully recognize that all mains 
4 
greater than 2 inches results from the aggregation of loads and this results in the need for 
5 
larger diameter mains.  As a result, large diameter mains are a direct function of load and 
6 
not customers.  In order to achieve a more equitable allocation of these costs, a use per 
7 
customer for the large customers is derived.  This use per customer is then used to divide 
8 
the consumption of each customer class that was assigned costs for 2-inch and below 
9 
(Residential and Small Commercial) to derive an equivalent customer count for each of 
10 
these classes. The classes other than those assigned cost for 2-inch and below will use 
11 
their respective customer count for the development of the Mains above 2 inches 
12 
customer allocation factor.  See Schedule PMN-10 for the development of this allocation 
13 
factor.

DEPRECIATION STUDY

297


--- Page 298 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 5 of 15 
Q. 
Are you familiar with the National Association of Regulatory Utility 
Commissioners' definition of depreciation? 
A. 
Yes.  The definition of depreciation adopted by the National Association of Regulatory 
Utility Commissioners (“NARUC”) is: 
“Depreciation”, as applied to depreciable utility plant, means the loss in 
service value not restored by current maintenance incurred in connection 
with the consumption or prospective retirement of utility plant in the 
course of service from causes which are known to be in current operation 
and against which the utility is not protected by insurance.  Among the 
causes to be given consideration are wear and tear, decay, action of the 
elements, inadequacy, obsolescence, changes in the art, changes in 
demand and requirements of public authorities.
The PSC is a member of NARUC. 
Another commonly referenced definition of depreciation is that of the American Institute 
of Certified Public Accounts (“AICPA”): 
Depreciation accounting is a system of accounting which aims to 
distribute the cost or other basic value of tangible capital assets, less 
salvage (if any) over the estimated useful life of the unit (which may be a 
group of assets) in a systematic and rational manner.  It is a process of 
allocation, not of valuation.  Depreciation for the year is the portion of the 
total charge under such a system that is allocated to the year.  Although 
the allocation may properly take into account occurrences during the 
year, it is not intended to be a measurement of the effect of all such 
occurrences.
The two foregoing citations are found on Pages 13 and 14, respectively, of “Public Utility 
Depreciation Practices,” August 1996, by the NARUC Staff Subcommittee on 
Depreciation. 
298


--- Page 299 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 6 of 15 
In my opinion, the AICPA definition helps clarify the NARUC definition in that it brings 
to the description the process of allocation of cost. 
Q.
What is the purpose of the periodic book depreciation rate studies, such as that
which you performed for CNG?
A.
Consistent with the definitions above, the purpose of depreciation studies is to develop
depreciation accrual rates reflective of engineering judgment, current industry and
specific company experience, and current projections for the future, relative to the
particular depreciable assets under study.  The objective of depreciation as an element of
the cost of service is to provide for the appropriate and equitable recovery of the
investments in depreciable assets over a life term that assures the full recovery of the
investments less estimated net salvage.  Net salvage is the gross salvage less those costs
relating to the removal or retirement of assets.
Q.
What procedures did you employ in compiling your depreciation studies?
A.
The first step was to create the depreciation study databases.  CNG provided MAC with
the necessary property accounting history, annual additions, annual retirements, plant
balances, adjustments and transfers to create a complete database history.
Q.
Please continue.
A.
We analyzed the historical data using computerized statistical routines and evaluated the
output by considering the indications from the statistical analyses, input from CNG’s
management, the character of the depreciable assets, experience with like assets, and
engineering knowledge and judgment.  Final calculations and life estimates were then
299


--- Page 300 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 7 of 15 
made to develop the recommended whole life accrual rates for each category of plant as 
shown in the Depreciation Study (Schedule PMN-2) sections entitled “Schedules” at 
Schedule A. 
Q. 
You previously referred to “statistical analyses.”  Would you please explain what is 
meant by this term? 
A. 
We are referring to the Simulated Plant Record (“SPR”) - Balances (“BAL”) method of 
life analysis, a well-known and accepted analysis employed in depreciation studies.  This 
analysis is used as a tool to assist us in the estimation of investment life.  Whenever 
records of annual additions, annual retirements and year-end account balances are 
available, an SPR-BAL analysis can be undertaken.  The SPR-BAL analyses were 
undertaken for all accounts with the exception of a portion of accounts relating to a new 
category we have identified as Leak Prone Pipe (“LPP”), as detailed in Schedule A of the 
Depreciation Study. 
The simulated year-end balances to which we matched the Company-observed year-end 
balances are based upon the “H” curves.  These curves were developed by Mr. Bradford 
Kimball of the New York PSC in 1947 and are based on a normal distribution of 
retirements (bell curve).  These curves are similar in shape and purpose to the more 
widely accepted and used Iowa curves. 
The SPR life analyses of property history can sometimes provide us with an estimate of 
the historical life of plant investments, possibly a starting point in the life estimation 
process; however, it must be noted that life analysis is not life estimation.  Unfortunately, 
300


--- Page 301 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 8 of 15 
life analysis can only provide an indication as to what has happened in the past.  Our need 
is to estimate what will occur in the future; i.e., we must predict the future, not merely 
measure the past. 
Q.
In evaluating the SPR-BAL analyses, you previously stated that MAC also
considered input from Corning.  What type of information did MAC consider?
A.
We conferred with Corning to determine if there were any occurrences, changes in
policy, procedure, equipment or practices that might impact service life, salvage or
removal cost associated with depreciable assets.  The major consideration was to
determine whether indications of the past would likely be representative of the near-term
future.
Q.
Can you give any examples of specific input provided by Corning that influenced
your life estimates?
A.
Yes.  We were advised that Corning has been installing automated meter reading using
Encoder, Receiver, Transmitter (“ERTS”) technology.  As a result, we recognized a much
shorter life for this type of electronic metering, Account 381.10.
Q.
Are there any other considerations that you incorporated in your analyses?
A.
Yes.  The Company is currently ten years into an extensive LPP replacement program
that is projected to be completed in approximately 7 years.  The Company is replacing
approximately 11 miles of mains per year.  As of December 31, 2018 there are about 71
miles consisting of bare and coated unprotected steel mains remaining to be replaced.
301


--- Page 302 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 9 of 15 
Corning’s service replacement is due to the LPP replacement program.  As of December 
31, 2018 there are approximately 1,471 services remaining that are part of the LPP 
replacement program using the same test period as the deprecation study.

A.

account was then further separated where the LPP pipe cost and associated reserve

relating to LPP were identified and noted in the depreciation study report.  With the 
balance by account shown on the Accrual Rate Schedule A, on Page 1, in the category of 
AMORTIZED PLANT-LEAK PRONE PIPE PROGRAM.

Q. 
What are the most prevalent approaches used in developing accrual rates? 
A. 
The depreciation process consists of selecting one of the more prevalent utility categories 
from each of the following three areas to develop a complete system in a study of utility 
plant:

Q. 
What system was used to develop the proposed accrual rates? 
A. 
The accrual rates were derived by using a straight line method, broad group average 
service life procedure and a whole life depreciation technique for each plant account as 
follows: 
Whole Life Accrual Rate   = 
100% - Net Salvage (NS%) 
Average Service Life
 
This is the depreciation system that is used by the Commission. 
Q. 
Your answers to previous questions indicate judgment and experience are 
significant elements in life estimation and in the interpretation of statistical analyses.  
Do other depreciation experts and authoritative sources concur? 
A. 
Yes, the literature is unambiguous on this point.  For example, the New York State 
Department of Public Service publication, “Computer Supported Property Mortality 
Studies,” published in 1971, at page I.1 states: 
The purpose of an actuarial mortality study of public utility property is to 
make a statistical determination of a representative life table and average 
service life.  The method used to derive these quantities in this report is 
that of smoothing and extending the retirement ratios. 
It must be clearly understood that the computer procedure explained in 
Section IWE accomplishes electronically only those computations which 
have had to be done manually, and nothing else.  Because of the 
computer’s large storage capacity and extremely fast running time, it is 
able to calculate a great deal more than has ever been obtained manually 
in the past. 
303


--- Page 304 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 11 of 15 
The computer exercises no judgment, reflects no opinions or company 
policies and does not forecast the future.  The computer programs are 
merely the results of applying certain mathematical formulae to a set of 
statistics obtained from accounting records – and, based on these data 
and formulae give an indication of what has been the retirement 
experience of the past and what would be the future life pattern if the same 
experience were constant over the entire life of the surviving property 
under study. 
Under no circumstances should it be construed that a specific indicated 
service life and life table developed by this computer process must 
necessarily be used as the life table and average service life in arriving at 
a final estimate of annual and accrued depreciation.  Stress is placed on 
the fact that the selected life table and average service life finally used, 
whether or not developed by program PSU-2 or PSU-2A must be the 
engineer’s best estimate for the property under study. 
In summary, life estimation considers the blending of many factors, including informed 
judgment, when predicting future expected lives of the Company’s various asset 
categories. 
Q.
Do regulatory commissions generally recognize that the use of judgment is part of
any depreciation study?
A.
Yes, they do.  It is my experience that most commissions have long recognized that
judgment is an important aspect of determining proper accrual rates in any depreciation
study.  The NARUC manual of Public Utility Depreciation Practices itself also presents a
brief discussion at page 126 that includes the following:
Informed judgment is a term used to define the subjective portion of the 
depreciation study process.  It is based on a combination of general 
experience, knowledge of the properties and a physical inspection, 
information gathered throughout the industry, and other factors which 
assist the analyst in making a knowledgeable estimate.... 
The analyst’s role in performing the study is to review the results and 
determine if they represent the mortality characteristics of the property.  
Using judgment, the analyst considers such things as personal experience, 
304


--- Page 305 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 12 of 15 
maintenance policies, past company studies, and other company owned 
equipment to determine if the stub curve represents this class of property. 
Q. 
What is the total CNG composite annual accrual rate which results from your 
Depreciation Study? 
A. 
The composite result of the proposed straight line, whole life individual account rates 
detailed in the Depreciation Study (Schedule PMN-2) is 2.83% and detailed for each 
account on Schedule A, column 8 of the report.  These proposed accrual rates do not 
include an amortization of the calculated variance shown in column 13 which are the 
differences (variances) between the actual booked depreciation reserves and our 
computed (theoretical) reserves.  This reserve variance is less than 10% of the theoretical 
reserve and less than 1% of the Total Depreciable Gas Plant. 
Q. 
Do the depreciation accrual rates you propose result in higher depreciation expense 
than that derived using the existing authorized depreciation accrual rates? 
A. 
Yes.  Using the same December 31, 2018 account balances, the proposed accrual rates 
result in a depreciation expense which is slightly higher than currently being recognized.  
On Schedule B, the proposed annual depreciation accrual expense is $2,514,870 as 
compared to $1,989,361 using the existing accrual rates.  This results in a $525,509 
increase in annual depreciation expense from the existing approved level. 
Q. 
Please elaborate upon the Net Salvage estimates used in determining your proposed 
accrual rates.
305


--- Page 306 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 13 of 15 
A.
Net salvage is one of several factors used in the derivation of each of the proposed
accrual rates presented in the Depreciation Study, Schedule PMN-2.  Net salvage is the
resulting difference between the gross salvage of an asset when it is disposed less its
associated cost of removal from service.
Q.
Is Net Salvage an important aspect to establishing reasonable and equitable
depreciation accrual rates?
A.
Yes it is.  Net salvage is an important cost that must be recovered in an equitable manner
over the useful life of an asset from those customers who benefit from the use and service
of an asset.  To defer the proper recovery of these costs until much later at retirement will
introduce a subsidy to existing customers by the recovery of these costs from only future
customers who may in fact only use an asset for a very small portion of its life.
Q.
Have you presented the Net Salvage impact in your Depreciation Study?
A.
The net salvage percent has been detailed for each account in column 6 of Schedule A.
In addition, a separate calculation has also been provided in column 14 for identifying the
cost of removal component contained in each proposed accrual rate shown in column 8.
Q.
Did you conduct an analysis of the Corning Natural Gas utility plant as affected by
New York State’s aggressive goals to limit or eliminate carbon emissions by the year
2050?
A.
Yes I did.  Those results are presented in Schedule C of Schedule PMN-2.
306


--- Page 307 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 14 of 15 
Q. 
How was the average service life for these plant balances determined in light of the
aggressive goals to limit or eliminate carbon emissions by the year 2050?
A. 
When performing the theoretical reserve analysis, if the results of the theoretical reserve 
indicate a remaining life of 30 years or greater for a specific plant account balance, the 
Average Service Life (“ASL”) is set at 30 years.  If the results of the theoretical reserve 
indicate a remaining life less than 30 years, the ASL is set at the calculated remaining 
life. 
Q. 
What is the impact on the accrual rates? 
A. 
Depreciation accrual rates will be increased and depreciation will be accelerated due to 
the lower ASL. 
Q. 
What is the total CNG composite annual accrual rate which results from Schedule 
C? 
A. 
The composite annual accrual rate is 4.75% and detailed for each account in column 8 of 
Schedule C of Schedule PMN-2. 
Q. 
Do the proposed accrual rates in column 8 of Schedule C of Schedule PMN-2 
include amortization of the calculated variance shown in column 13? 
A. 
No, the accrual rates in column 8 do not include the amortization of the calculated 
variance.  In addition, the amortized amounts do not include any additions or retirements 
307


--- Page 308 ---
Testimony of Paul M. Normand 
Page 15 of 15 
during the 30-year period.  This approach is proposed in order to be conservative in the 
costs estimates to be recovered based on currently known data. 
Q. 
Do the depreciation accrual rates you proposed in Schedule C of Schedule PMN-2 
result in a higher depreciation expense than in Schedule A of Schedule PMN-2? 
A. 
Yes they do.  On Schedule C, the proposed annual depreciation accrual expense is 
$4,229,427 as compared to $2,514,870 in Schedule A.  This results in a $1,714,557 
increase in annual depreciation expense due to the aggressive goals to limit or eliminate 
carbon emissions by the year 2050. 
Q. 
Do the depreciation accrual rates you proposed in Schedule C of Schedule PMN-2 
include all of the recoverable costs for Corning? 
A. 
No they do not.  One of the remaining costs not included is the on-going accelerated 
replacement costs associated with LPP that will be incurred in the next 7 years which will 
add a considerable amount of costs to be recovered over the next 30 years.  We expect 
that these costs will be more fully defined in the Company’s next depreciation study. 
IV. 
CONCLUSION 
Q. 
Does this complete your testimony regarding depreciation? 
A. 
Yes.

Q.

7 
A. 
NPA screening criteria are a set of requirements
8

9 
an NPA project when all the criteria are met.  
10 
When considering a capital project, the Company 
11 
must compare the project against the screening

13 
screening criteria, the Company must attempt to 
14 
develop an NPA project to implement in lieu of 
15

16 
Corning may optionally attempt to develop NPA 
17 
projects for those traditional capital 
18 
investments which do not meet all the criteria, 
19 
however, it would not be obligated to do so.

one fiscal year.  In the event these screening

Depreciation 
21 
Q. 
Panel, please explain the terms “net salvage” 
22 
and “depreciation”, as they are used in 
23 
ratemaking. 
24 
414


--- Page 415 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
SIOP 
17 
A. 
Net salvage is any cash received for an asset
1 
removed from service, less the cost to remove 
2 
it.  Depreciation is a method of recovering 
3 
capital cost, less net salvage, related to plant 
4 
in service over the plant’s expected useful 
5 
life. 
6 
Q. 
Please explain the term “average service life”.
7 
A. 
The average service life is the time period, in
8 
years, over which the original cost of plant 
9 
should be depreciated.   
10 
Q. 
Please define “depreciation rate” and
11 
“depreciation expense”. 
12 
A. 
A depreciation rate is a percentage rate applied
13 
to the gross plant in service, by account, to 
14 
determine the annual depreciation expense.  The 
15 
annual depreciation expense is the product of 
16 
gross plant-in-service and the applicable 
17 
depreciation rate and allows for the recovery of 
18 
an investment, less net salvage, over the 
19 
expected life of the investment. 
20 
Q. 
Did Corning file a depreciation study in this
21 
proceeding? 
22 
A. 
Yes, the Company performed a depreciation study
23 
as presented in the testimony of Paul M. Normand 
24 
415


--- Page 416 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
SIOP 
18 
- Depreciation.  The Company’s proposed
1 
depreciation accrual rates are shown in
2 
Exhibit___(CNG-11, Schedule A).
3 
Q.

7

Corning’s accrual rates were developed by using
11

14 
Q.

15

16 
A. 
Under the whole life technique, the depreciation
17 
rate is calculated using the following formula: 
18 
Rate = (1-Net Salvage)/(Average Service Life).  
19 
The rate is then multiplied by the gross plant 
20 
to obtain the depreciation expense for 
21 
ratemaking purposes.  Composite rates are then 
22 
calculated, which are weighted average rates 
23 
based on gross plant in service as of a specific

III.
REGULATORY GUIDELINES AND FINANCIAL 
CONSIDERATIONS 
Please describe the guiding principles to be used in establishing the cost 
13 
of capital for a regulated utility. 
14 
The United States Supreme Court’s precedent-setting Hope and Bluefield
15 
cases established the standards for determining the reasonableness of a 
16 
utility’s allowed ROE.  Among the standards established by the Court in 
17 
those cases are:  (1) consistency with the returns on equity investments in 
18 
other businesses having similar or comparable risks; (2) adequacy of the 
19 
return to support credit quality and access to capital; and (3) an 
20 
understanding that the means of arriving at a fair return are not controlling, 
21 
only that the end result leads to just and reasonable rates.3
22 
3
Federal Power Commission v. Hope Natural Gas Co., 320 U.S. 591 (1944) (“Hope”);

Commission’s goal in opening the GFP was to reduce controversy around 
1

4

Do the principles and intentions of the RD in the GFP require 
1 
adherence to a static formula? 
2 
No.  The GFP and RD did not require rote adherence to a static formula; 
3 
rather, they promoted some basic principles and afforded parties the 
4 
flexibility to investigate approaches to address changing financial market 
5 
conditions.  The RD recognized the benefit of using multiple approaches for 
6 
setting ROE and although it found benefits to a preferred convention for 
7 
setting ROE, it did not bar parties from introducing new cost of capital 
8 
estimation methods or weightings and specifically recognized that there 
9 
may be circumstances where this would be superior.  Capital market 
10 
conditions vary widely over time and each ROE methodology (DCF and 
11 
CAPM) may be affected differently by identical conditions.  The effect of 
12 
these conditions on ROE must be assessed and interpreted by the 
13 
practitioner to determine if their effects are directionally appropriate and are 
14 
of a reasonable magnitude.  Accordingly, it is incumbent on the practitioner 
15 
to review the results of the analyses and exercise judgment as to how to 
16 
weight those results in the overall ROE determination.  A review of the RD 
17 
reveals that the Commission expressed some uncertainty around the correct 
18 
level of weighting and certainly indicated a willingness to revisit its 
19 
proposed weightings in the future.  It is particularly fitting that the 
20 
Commission, which is seeking to update the traditional utility regulatory 
21 
model with new, innovative approaches suitable to current industry 
22 
circumstances in the New York Reforming the Energy Vision (“NY REV”)

17 
Is flexibility of approach and judgment important to ROE 
18 
determination? 
19 
Yes, it is.  When faced with the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts 
20 
are inclined to gather and evaluate as much relevant data (both quantitative 
21 
and qualitative) as can be reasonably analyzed.  Analysts and academics 
22 
understand that ROE models are tools to be used in the ROE estimation 
23 
process, and that strict adherence to any single approach, or the specific 
24 
459


--- Page 460 ---
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 15 of 97 
results of any single approach, can lead to flawed conclusions.  No model 
1 
can exactly pinpoint the correct return on equity; rather, each model brings 
2 
its own perspective and set of inputs that inform the estimate of ROE.  That 
3 
position is consistent with the Hope finding that “[u]nder the statutory 
4 
standard of ‘just and reasonable,’ it is the result reached, not the method 
5 
employed, which is controlling.”9 
6 
7 
Though each model brings a different perspective and adds depth to the 
8 
analysis, each model also has its own set of inherent weaknesses and should 
9 
not be relied upon individually without corroboration from other 
10 
approaches.  Changes to inputs as a result of changes in economic 
11 
conditions could have widely different effects on the results of the various 
12 
analyses.   
13 
14 
Regardless of which analyses are performed to estimate the investor’s 
15 
required return on equity, the analyst must apply judgment to assess the 
16 
reasonableness of results and to determine the best weighting to apply to 
17 
results under prevailing capital market conditions.  No one model can 
18 
reliably and consistently estimate the cost of capital that meets the fairness 
19 
standard of Hope and Bluefield in all market conditions.

IV.
  CAPITAL MARKET CONDITIONS 
Why is it important to analyze capital market conditions? 
1 
The ROE estimation models rely on market data that are either specific to 
2 
the proxy group, in the case of the DCF model, or the expectations of market 
3 
risk, in the case of the CAPM.  The results of the ROE estimation models 
4 
can be affected by prevailing market conditions at the time the analysis is 
5 
performed.  While the ROE that is established in a rate proceeding is 
6 
intended to be forward-looking, the analyst uses current and projected 
7 
market data, specifically stock prices, dividends, growth rates and interest 
8 
rates in the ROE estimation models to estimate the required return for the 
9 
subject company.  It is important to consider whether the assumptions relied 
10 
on in the current market or the projected data are sustainable over the period 
11 
that the recommended ROE would be in effect.  If investors do not expect 
12 
current market conditions to be sustained in the future, it is possible that the 
13 
ROE estimation models will not provide an accurate estimate of investors’ 
14 
required return during that rate period. 
15 
16 
What factors are affecting the cost of equity for regulated utilities in 
17 
the current and prospective capital markets? 
18 
The cost of equity for regulated utility companies is being affected by 
19 
several factors in the current and prospective capital markets, including: (1) 
20 
valuations of utility stocks that are at historically high levels, which has an 
21 
inverse relationship to dividend yields; (2) recent market uncertainty, its 
22

current effect on interest rates, and long-term expectations for interest rates; 
1 
and (3) recent Federal tax reform.  In this section, we discuss each of these 
2 
factors and how it affects the models used to estimate the cost of equity for 
3 
regulated utilities.

A. THE EFFECT OF MARKET CONDITIONS ON VALUATIONS
6 
How has the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy affected capital
7 
markets in recent years?
8 
Extraordinary and persistent federal intervention in capital markets
9 
artificially lowered government bond yields after the Great Recession of
10 
2008-2009, as the Federal Open Market Committee (“FOMC”) used
11 
monetary policy (both reductions in short-term interest rates and purchases
12 
of Treasury bonds and mortgage-backed securities) to stimulate the U.S.
13 
economy.  As a result of very low or zero returns on short-term government
14 
bonds, yield-seeking investors have moved into longer-term instruments,
15 
bidding up prices and reducing yields on those investments.  As investors
16 
have moved along the risk spectrum in search of higher yields that meet
17 
their return requirements, there has been increased demand for dividend-
18 
paying equities, such as natural gas and electric utility stocks.
19 
20 
How has the period of abnormally low interest rates affected the 
21 
valuations and dividend yields of utility shares? 
22 
The Federal Reserve’s accommodative monetary policy has caused 
23 
investors to seek alternatives to the historically low interest rates available

2

5

6

7

8

10

11 
company B is growing at a rate of 15 percent, then on a relative valuation 
12 
basis company B is the better investment.     
13 
14

15

16

17 
Reserve following the Great Recession of 2008-2009.16  While the PEG 
18 
ratio has declined in recent years due to the Federal Reserve’s shift to 
19 
normalize monetary policy, the PEG ratio for the S&P Utilities Index is still 
20 
above the historical average.  In general, stocks with lower long-term PEG 
21 
ratios are considered better values.  As the PEG ratio increases above the

C. EFFECT OF TAX REFORM ON THE ROE AND CAPITAL STRUCTURE
12 
Are there other factors that should be considered in determining the
13 
cost of equity for Corning Gas?
14 
Yes.  The effect of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (“TCJA”) should also be
15 
considered in the determination of the cost of equity.  The credit rating
16 
agencies have commented on the effect of the TCJA on regulated utilities.
17 
In summary, the TCJA is expected to reduce utility revenues due to the
18 
lower federal income taxes, the end of bonus depreciation, and the
19 
requirement to return excess Accumulated Deferred Income Taxes
20 
(“ADIT”).  This change in revenue is expected to reduce Funds From
21 
Operations (“FFO”) metrics across the sector, and absent regulatory
22 
477


--- Page 478 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 33 of 97 
mitigation strategies, is expected to lead to weaker credit metrics and 
1 
negative ratings actions for some utilities.27
2 
3 
Have credit or equity analysts commented on the effect of the TCJA on 
4 
utilities? 
5 
Yes.  Each of the credit rating agencies has indicated that the TCJA would 
6 
have an overall negative credit impact on regulated operating companies of 
7 
utilities and their holding companies due to the reduction in cash flow that 
8 
results from the change in the federal tax rate and the loss of bonus 
9 
depreciation. 
10 
11 
Moody’s noted that the rates that regulators allow utilities to charge 
12 
customers is based on a cost-plus model, with tax expense being one of the 
13 
pass-through items.  Utilities will collect less income tax at a lower rate, 
14 
reducing revenue.  In addition, with the loss of bonus depreciation, the 
15 
timing of future cash tax payments will be accelerated.  Therefore, utilities 
16 
will collect less tax revenue as a result of the lower tax rate and retain less 
17 
of the collected taxes as a result of the loss of bonus depreciation.  All else 
18 
being equal, the changes will have a negative effect on utility cash flows 
19 
and will, ultimately, negatively impact the utilities’ ability to fund ongoing 
20 
operations and capital improvement programs. 
21 
22 
27

V.
PROXY GROUP SELECTION
Please explain why have you used a group of proxy companies to 
15 
estimate the cost of equity for the Company? 
16 
In this proceeding, we are estimating the cost of equity for a company that 
17 
has rate-regulated, natural gas distribution utility operations in New York.  
18 
Because ROE is a market-based concept and the Company is not publicly 
19 
traded, it is necessary to establish a group of companies that is both publicly 
20 
traded and comparable to Corning Gas in certain fundamental business and 
21 
financial respects to serve as proxies in the ROE estimation process.  The 
22 
483


--- Page 484 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 39 of 97 
proxy companies used in our analyses all possess a set of operating and risk 
1 
characteristics that are substantially comparable to the Company and thus 
2 
provide a reasonable basis for the derivation and assessment of the 
3 
Company’s ROE. 
4 
5 
In utility rate proceedings before the Commission over the past 25 years 
6 
(since the RD in the GFP),32 the Commission has endorsed the use of proxy 
7 
groups for the purpose of determining utility ROEs.  Because proxy 
8 
companies are now commonly used as the basis for estimating the utility 
9 
cost of equity, the primary objective of the screening process is to establish 
10 
a group of companies that is as comparable as possible to the subject 
11 
company with respect to fundamental financial and business risks.  While 
12 
the determination of an appropriate ROE necessarily requires a degree of 
13 
informed judgment, the careful selection of a risk-comparable proxy group 
14 
serves to mitigate the extent to which subjective assessments must be 
15 
applied. 
16

Please provide a summary profile of the Company. 
18

19 
services to approximately 15,000 residential, commercial, industrial, and

How did you select the companies included in your proxy groups? 
1 
The Commission has historically relied on proxy groups generally 
2 
comprised of electric utilities even for the purposes of establishing the ROE 
3 
for a natural gas distribution utility.  In recognition of that practice and 
4 
taking into consideration that Corning is a natural gas distribution company, 
5 
we began with the companies that Value Line classifies as “Electric 
6 
Utilities” and “Natural Gas Distribution Companies.”  That combined group 
7 
includes 48 domestic U.S. utilities.  We simultaneously applied the 
8 
following screening criteria to establish a risk-comparable Combined 
9 
Utility Proxy Group that includes electric utility companies and natural gas 
10 
distribution companies: 
11 

To ensure that information regarding the proxy group companies is
12 
consensus-based, we eliminated the companies that are not covered
13 
by at least two utility industry equity analysts;
14 

We eliminated companies that do not have investment grade
15

VI.
COST OF EQUITY ESTIMATION 
Please briefly discuss the ROE in the context of the regulated Rate of 
10 
Return. 
11 
The rate of return (“ROR”) for a regulated utility is based on its weighted 
12 
average cost of capital, in which the costs of the individual sources of capital 
13 
are weighted by their respective percentages of total capitalization of the 
14 
utility.  The ROE included in the ROR is weighted by the percentage of 
15 
common equity in the regulated utility’s ratemaking capital structure. 
16 
17 
How is the required ROE determined? 
18 
While the cost of debt can be directly observed, the cost of equity and the 
19 
required ROE are market-based and, therefore, must be estimated based on 
20 
observable market information.  The required ROE is determined by using 
21 
one or more analytical techniques that rely on market data to quantify 
22 
493


--- Page 494 ---
Q• 
A. 
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 49 of 97 
investor expectations regarding the range of required equity returns.  
1 
Informed judgment is applied, based on the results of those analyses, to 
2 
determine where within the range of results the cost of equity for a company 
3 
falls.  As a general proposition, the key consideration in determining the 
4 
cost of equity is to ensure that the methodologies employed reasonably 
5 
reflect investors’ views of the financial markets, the proxy group 
6 
companies, and the subject company’s risk profile. 
7 
8 
What methods did you use to determine the Company’s cost of equity?  
9 
Consistent with Commission precedent, we used the DCF model and 
10 
CAPM as the primary approaches.  In establishing our recommended ROE, 
11 
we relied on a multi-stage form of the DCF model, and, consistent with the 
12 
Commission’s stated preference, we used both the traditional form of the 
13 
CAPM, as well as the Zero-Beta form of that model.  In both forms of the 
14 
CAPM, we incorporated a forward-looking measure of the Market Risk 
15 
Premium.  
16 
17 
Why do you believe it is important to use more than one analytical 
18 
approach? 
19 
Because the cost of equity is not directly observable, it must be estimated 
20 
based on both quantitative and qualitative information.  When faced with 
21 
the task of estimating the cost of equity, analysts and investors are inclined 
22 
to gather and evaluate as much relevant data as reasonably can be 
23 
analyzed.  As a result, a number of models have been developed to estimate 
24 
494


--- Page 495 ---
Q• 
A. 
Testimony of Ann E. Bulkley and Christopher M. Wall
Page 50 of 97 
the cost of equity.  For that reason, we use multiple approaches to estimate 
1 
the cost of equity.  As a practical matter, however, all of the models 
2 
available for estimating the cost of equity are subject to limiting 
3 
assumptions or other methodological constraints.  Consequently, many 
4 
finance texts recommend using multiple approaches when estimating the 
5 
cost of equity.  For example, Copeland, Koller, and Murrin40 suggest using 
6 
the CAPM and Arbitrage Pricing Theory model, while Brigham and 
7 
Gapenski41 recommend the CAPM, DCF, and “bond yield plus risk 
8 
premium” approaches.42  
9

11 
CAPM models?  
12 
As discussed in Section IV, the results of the DCF model are understating 
13 
the forward-looking cost of equity.  The CAPM method offers some balance 
14 
to the sensitivity of the DCF model to low Treasury bond yields.  However, 
15 
low interest rates also impact the CAPM in two ways: (1) if the risk-free 
16 
rate is based on historical average yields on Treasury bonds, it understates 
17 
the forward-looking risk-free rate, and (2) if the market risk premium is 
18 
based on historical returns on large company stocks minus the historical

A. DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW MODEL
6 
Please describe the DCF approach.
7 
The DCF approach is based on the theory that a stock’s current market price
8 
represents the present value of all expected future cash flows.  In its most
9 
general form, the DCF model is expressed as follows in Equation [1]:
10 
[1]
11 
Where P0 represents the current market stock price, D1 … Dn are all 
12 
expected future dividends, and r is the discount rate, or required ROE.  As 
13 
discussed below, we have not included the constant growth form of the DCF 
14 
model, but instead have focused on a multi-stage form of the DCF model.   
15 
16 
Please generally describe the DCF model you relied on.  
17 
The multi-stage DCF model is an extension of the constant growth form that 
18 
enables the analyst to specify growth rates over multiple stages.  As with 
19 
the constant growth form of the DCF model, the multi-stage form defines 
20 
the cost of equity as the discount rate that sets the current price equal to the 
21 
discounted value of future cash flows.  A multi-stage DCF model addresses 
22

Page 53 of 97 
the possibility that mean five-year growth rates may not be reasonable in 
1 
perpetuity and that payout ratios could vary over time. 
2 
3 
Please describe the structure of the multi-stage DCF model.  
4 
The multi-stage DCF model that we have used sets the proxy company’s 
5 
current stock price equal to the present value of future cash flows received 
6 
over three time periods.  In all three periods, cash flows are equal to the 
7 
annual dividend payments that stockholders receive.  The first period is a 
8 
short-term growth period that consists of the first five years; the second 
9 
period is a transition period from the short-term growth rate to the long-term 
10 
growth rate that occurs over five years (i.e., years 6 through 10); and the 
11 
third period is a long-term growth period that begins in year 11 and 
12 
continues in perpetuity.  The ROE is then calculated as the rate of return 
13 
that results from the initial stock investment and the dividend payments over 
14 
the analytical period. 
15

17

18 
prior cases.43  The two-stage model that the Commission has relied on and 
19 
the multi-stage model that we rely on both define the cost of equity as the 
20 
discount rate that sets the current stock price equal to the discounted value
