THE PANEL’S METHODOLOGY AND FORECAST 
4 
Q.  What methodology did this Panel use to develop
5 
its forecast? 
6 
A.  We used econometric modelling methodology to
7 
develop our forecast. 
8 
Q. 
Please describe the basic functioning of
9 
econometric modelling methodology. 
10 
A. 
Econometric models relate gas sales or number of
11 
customers to a set of explanatory or independent 
12 
variables, economic and demographic, weather, 
13 
and other seasonal variables. Economic and 
14 
demographic variables include those such as 
15 
population, price of electricity, personal 
16 
income, or employment. Weather variables are 
17 
represented by heating degree days.  Seasonal 
18 
variables may adjust for calendar month or other 
19 
billing cycle related variations. The 
20 
relationship between these explanatory variables 
21 
and gas deliveries over time constitutes the 
22 
structural component of the econometric 
23 
forecasting models.  Also, because gas customer 
24 
1044


--- Page 1045 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
Staff Forecasting Panel 
11 
and usage data are time-series data, econometric 
1 
models may also include a non-structural 
2 
component. 
3 
Q. 
Please explain the non-structural component of
4 
an econometric forecasting model. 
5 
A. 
The non-structural component is represented by a
6 
procedure that relates the contemporaneous 
7 
values and estimation errors of a time-series to 
8 
its past values and estimation errors in the 
9 
model. This is done via the addition of moving 
10 
average and autoregressive variables to the 
11 
model structure. This component is included to 
12 
capture the remaining variations in gas sales or 
13 
number of customers, stemming from time trend, 
14 
seasonality, as well as serial correlations in 
15 
residual errors. 
16 
Q. 
How is an econometric model estimated?
17 
A. 
An econometric model is estimated using
18 
regression techniques on historical data. 
19 
Econometric estimation techniques attempt to 
20 
minimize the amount of variation in the gas 
21 
delivery and customer data that is not explained 
22 
by the structural and non-structural explanatory 
23 
variables in the model. An econometric forecast 
24 
1045


--- Page 1046 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
 
Staff Forecasting Panel 
 
 
12 
 
uses the estimated historical relationship 
1 
between the variables and applies it to 
2 
forecasts of the explanatory variables in order 
3 
to produce an estimate of future energy 
4 
deliveries or customers. 
5 
Q. 
Why is an econometric modeling approach better 
6 
than the Company’s subjective method? 
7 
A. 
Under an econometric modeling approach, the use 
8 
of natural gas in a historical period is not 
9 
treated as a standalone phenomenon.  Rather, the 
10 
use of gas is presumed to be related to factors 
11 
such as consumers’ and business’ economic 
12 
behavior and activities using their gas 
13 
appliance and equipment.  Economic theory posits 
14 
that use of natural gas in a historical period 
15 
is driven by factors which include the cost of 
16 
gas as well as consumers’ and businesses’ 
17 
wellbeing.  Econometric modelling uses 
18 
statistical techniques to estimate the relative 
19 
impact of such explanatory drivers on gas usage.  
20 
Our econometric models are estimated by 
21 
multivariate regression techniques on historical 
22 
data over a five-year period to simultaneously 
23 
determine the effect of weather and economic 
24 
1046


--- Page 1047 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
 
Staff Forecasting Panel 
 
 
13 
 
variables on the variation in gas usage.  In 
1 
addition, as indicated by the lagged 
2 
relationships and non-structural components in 
3 
our econometric models, the estimated lagged 
4 
relationships and forecasting errors of the past 
5 
can be fed back into the models and refined 
6 
parameter estimates can be generated to improve 
7 
future forecasting results.  The forecasting 
8 
confidence levels can also be generated.  
9 
Therefore, our method is dynamic, probabilistic, 
10 
and objective, rather than the static, 
11 
deterministic, and subjective approach used by 
12 
the Company.  
13 
Q. 
Please describe the Panel’s forecasting models. 
14 
A. 
Our forecast is based on four sales models 
15 
consists of four sales forecasting models.  The 
16 
sales forecasting models are for service classes 
17 
SC 1, SC 3, SC 14, and SC 6.  In general, these 
18 
sales models have monthly billed sales in 
19 
million cubic feet (MCF) as the dependent 
20 
variable on the left-hand side of the equation.  
21 
The explanatory variables on the right-hand side 
22 
of the models include the average real price of 
23 
natural gas, the number of customers in the 
24 
1047


--- Page 1048 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
Staff Forecasting Panel 
14 
service class, heating degree days, and number 
1 
of days in a calendar month.  We also developed 
2 
two customer forecasting models for the 
3 
explanatory customer variable in the SC 1 and SC 
4 
3 sales forecasting models.  All sales and 
5 
customer models are estimated in semi-log linear 
6 
format, meaning that sales or customer count for 
7 
a service class is defined as a semi-log linear 
8 
function of a set of the specified explanatory 
9 
variables.  All models are estimated using the 
10 
monthly historical data from January 2015

The model specifications and statistical results

19 
forecast the forecasted values are summarized in 
20 
Exhibit__(SFP-2).

customers are more appropriately deflated by the

3

4 
and services.

Q. 
Please discuss the statistics results of your
6 
models. 
7 
A. 
In general, as shown on Exhibit___(SFP-4), the
8 
models perform well, and all the summary 
9 
statistics are very good.  First, most 
10 
explanatory variables included in the models 
11

12

14

15 
than 95 to 99 percent.  Also, all models have 
16 
high adjusted R-squared.  The R-squared 
17 
statistic, ranging from 0 to 1, measures the 
18 
degree of goodness-to-fit of the regression 
19 
model, with 0 being the least fit and 1 being 
20 
the best fit.  The adjusted R-squared of the six 
21 
models range 0.9549 to 0.9916, suggesting that 
22 
more than 95 to 99 percent of variations in gas 
23 
sales or number of customers are explained by 
24 
1050


--- Page 1051 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
Staff Forecasting Panel 
17 
the included explanatory variables. The Durbin-
1 
Watson (DW) statistics are between 1.6865 and 
2 
2.2133, indicating that they pass the serial 
3 
correlation test at a confidence of 95 or 99 
4 
percent.  All these statistics show that the 
5 
models perform well and have met the standard 
6 
criteria. 
7 
Q. 
How were the Panel’s forecasts for sales and
8 
customers generated from these models? 
9 
A. 
The predicted values for the explanatory
10 
variables for the forecasting period, from 
11 
January 2020 through January 2024 must be 
12 
obtained and input into the estimated model to 
13 
generate the forecast for sales and customer 
14 
counts.  For MCF forecasting models where the 
15 
number of customers is modelled as an 
16 
explanatory variable, we first run the customer 
17 
forecasting models to generate the customer 
18 
forecast before including that customer forecast 
19 
as an input into the MCF forecasting model.   
20 
Q. 
What did you assume for price of natural gas for
21 
the forecast? 
22 
A. 
We assume the real price stays the same during
23 
the forecasting period.  In other words, the 
24 
1051


--- Page 1052 ---
Case 20-G-0101 
 
Staff Forecasting Panel 
 
 
18 
 
nominal average cost of natural gas to retail 
1 
customers, including cost of services for 
2

3 
pace as inflation.  We make a such assumption 
4 
for the following reasons.  First, it is a 
5 
convenient assumption without our engaging any 
6

7

8 
Furthermore, in case there is significant price 
9

10 
always either rerun the model output with 
11

12 
which measures the percentage change in sales 
13 
per one percent of change in price, to calculate 
14 
the impact of price change.  Second, it is a 
15 
reasonable assumption.  There are indeed 
16 
correlations to certain degree between inflation 
17 
and energy cost.  In any event, the price of 
18 
energy is part of the total inflation basket.  
19 
Third, the increase in total nominal cost of 
20 
natural gas for the Corning customers for the

Q. 
Please explain the Panel’s method to determine 
2 
acceptable performance for this metric? 
3 
A. 
We have, generally, assumed that historical 
4 
averages represent a satisfactory level of 
5 
service, and targets are set using two standard 
6 
deviations from the Company’s historical average 
7 
performance.  In this case, the Company’s 
8 
historic five-year average is calculated at 
9 
90.8% and two standard deviations is calculated 
10 
at 3.1%. 
11 
Q. 
Why are two standard deviations used to develop 
12 
the CSS targets? 
13 
A. 
A performance result that is more than two 
14 
standard deviations from the average carries a 
15 
95 percent confidence level that the result is 
16 
not due to normal, random variations.  Such 
17 
actual performance result is therefore likely 
18 
due to utility actions.

may be arranged over the phone, via email, in 
5 
person, or by mail.

17 
electronically through a secure portal on the 
18 
utility’s website.  The customer can then print 
19 
the DPA and receive a hard copy in the mail from 
20 
the utility.

22 
the traditional hard copy DPA process? 
23 
1090

35

1

2

4

the DPA process.

FAIR RATE OF RETURN 
3 
Q. 
Earlier, the Panel mentioned that the fair rate 
4 
of return that it recommends will be used to 
5 
establish the Company’s revenue requirement.  
6 
Please explain what the Panel means by revenue 
7 
requirement. 
8 
A. 
In the context of Commission rate proceedings, 
9 
the revenue requirement is the dollar amount 
10 
required by a company to provide service during 
11 
a rate year.  It is the amount that will allow 
12 
the company to recover all of its reasonably 
13 
expected operating costs, including taxes and 
14 
depreciation.  In addition, the revenue 
15 
requirement includes a fair return that will 
16 
allow the utility the opportunity to recover the 
17 
cost of funds supplied to it by investors.  The 
18 
funds provided by these investors are necessary 
19 
for the company to finance its long-term utility 
20 
assets and working capital requirements, which 
21 
in the rate-setting context are referred to as 
22 
its “rate base.” 
23 
Q. 
Generally speaking, what is a fair rate of 
24 
1118


--- Page 1119 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
9 
return for a regulated utility? 
1 
A. 
A fair rate of return for a regulated utility is
2 
one that enables it to provide safe and adequate 
3 
service to its customers, while at the same time 
4 
assuring the company continuing support in the 
5 
capital markets for both its debt and equity 
6 
securities, at terms that are reasonable given 
7 
the company’s risk.  The fair rate of return, 
8 
therefore, allows the utility to recover its 
9 
prudently incurred cost of debt while providing 
10 
its common equity investors the opportunity to 
11 
earn a return that is commensurate with the risk 
12 
of their investment. 
13 
Q. 
How is a fair rate of return calculated?
14 
A. 
The fair rate of return for a utility company is
15 
calculated as the weighted average cost of the 
16 
individual components of its expected 
17 
capitalization during the rate year.  The two 
18 
primary sources are long-term debt and common 
19 
equity.  Customer deposits, while typically a 
20 
very small component, are almost always 
21 
reflected in the expected capitalization as well 
22 
because they are a relatively permanent and 
23 
stable source of capital employed by utilities.  
24 
1119


--- Page 1120 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
10 
 
Preferred stock and short-term debt are 
1 
sometimes a source of capital as well, although 
2 
in smaller proportions than either long-term 
3 
debt or common equity.  Since the Commission 
4 
uses a fully forecast rate year, it is also 
5 
important that the rate year capitalization 
6 
reflects the utility’s projected capital 
7 
requirements and is consistent with the goal of 
8 
achieving the optimal cost of capital, 
9 
particularly as it relates to the use of 
10 
leverage. 
11 
Q. 
How are the cost rates of the individual cost 
12 
components of capitalization typically 
13 
calculated? 
14 
A. 
The cost rates associated with a utility’s long-
15 
debt, short-term debt, and customer deposits are 
16 
relatively straightforward to ascertain.  The 
17 
embedded cost of debt, both long-term and short-
18 
term, can be readily calculated by examining the 
19 
contractual terms; i.e., the interest payments 
20 
for the debt.  The projected impact of the cost 
21 
of any new or incremental debt, however, 
22 
requires estimates using relevant market data.  
23 
The cost rate for customer deposits is simply a 
24 
1120


--- Page 1121 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
11 
 
matter of applying the cost rate that is 
1 
currently prescribed by the Commission.  The 
2 
cost of common equity, however, is neither 
3 
contractual nor prescribed by the Commission.  
4 
Its calculation is further complicated by the 
5 
fact that it cannot be directly observed, and 
6 
instead requires estimation and the opinion of 
7 
analysts.  
8 
Q. 
Is the cost of common equity typically more 
9 
expensive than the cost of long-term debt for a 
10 
utility?   
11 
A. 
Yes.  Even though both lenders and common equity 
12 
investors supply the utility with the funds it 
13 
needs to build and operate its system, the 
14 
common equity investors only earn a return after 
15 
the payment of all other expenses.  Because 
16 
these investors run the risk that their achieved 
17 
returns will not meet their expectations, the 
18 
return required by common equity investors is 
19 
usually higher than that of the utility’s long-
20 
term debt holders.  Exceptions may exist during 
21 
periods of disturbances in the market, such as 
22 
during the recessionary period of 1980 to 1982, 
23 
at which point the economy was beset with very 
24 
1121


--- Page 1122 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
12 
high inflation and volatile interest rates.  
1 
During that time, utility bond yields were at 
2 
least as high as the equity returns the 
3 
Commission allowed, and far above the returns 
4 
allowed by most state regulatory commissions.  
5 
Q. 
How can a utility’s cost of common equity be
6 
measured? 
7 
A. 
The return requirements of a utility’s common
8 
equity investors can only be gleaned through a 
9 
cost of equity analysis.  Generally, the 
10 
Commission has favored market-based 
11 
methodologies, such as the Discounted Cash Flow 
12 
(DCF) and the Capital Asset Pricing Model 
13 
(CAPM), to estimate the return required by 
14 
common equity investors.   
15 
CAPITAL STRUCTURE 
16 
Q. 
What does a company’s capital structure
17 
represent? 
18 
A. 
The capital structure is the mixture of types of
19 
capital, such as debt and equity, which a 
20 
company uses to finance its business; in the 
21 
case of a utility company, it is the capital 
22 
deployed to support its rate base.   
23

What was Corning’s actual capital structure on
24

3

4

Q. 
Please explain what the Panel means by “stand-
10

11 
A. 
When we say “stand-alone” capital structure, we 
12

13 
alone.  That is, without accounting for the 
14

15

Q. 
Please explain why there are both “stand-alone” 
19 
and parent company capitalizations. 
20 
A. 
A corporation is considered a utility holding 
21 
company if it owns 10% or more of the stock of 
22 
an electric or gas utility operating company.  
23 
Today, just as with electric utilities, nearly 
24 
1123

all investor-owned gas utilities are owned by 
1 
holding companies.  Corning is wholly-owned by 
2

3 
stock of Pike County Light & Power Company, a 
4 
combination electric and gas utility in 
5 
Pennsylvania, and it has investments in some 
6 
non-utility businesses as well.

Q.

16 
Corning’s projected capital structure was 
17

21 
Q.

22

23 
A. 
Corning’s projected capital structure for the
24 
1126

Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
17 
 
Rate Year is incorrect for six reasons: 1) the 
1 
omission of three of Corning’s currently

Q. 
Please explain the Company’s failure to 
12 
incorporate three of its outstanding loans. 
13 
A. 
Corning borrowed $3.13 million pursuant to a 10-
14 
year loan in 2019, as well as $300,000 pursuant 
15

16 
Corning also borrowed $970,000 from the Federal 
17

18 
(PPP).  None of these loans are reflected in the 
19

20 
capitalization. 
21 
Q. 
Please explain the Company’s failure to reflect 
22 
depreciation and deferred taxes as a source of 
23

24 
1127


--- Page 1128 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
18 
 
A. 
Corning’s capital structure forecast is based on 
1 
the erroneous assumption that capital 
2 
expenditures will be funded entirely with newly 
3 
raised capital and an increase in retained 
4 
earnings.  Rather, as is the case with any going 
5 
concern, a large portion of Corning’s capital 
6 
investment can be funded through depreciation 
7 
and deferred taxes, both of which are sources of 
8 
internally generated cash.  Only a piece of its 
9 
capital expenditures needs to be funded through 
10 
external sources or an increase in retained 
11 
earnings. 
12 
Q. 
Please explain the Company’s failure to account 
13 
for the need to refinance principal repayments. 
14 
A. 
Per the terms of its outstanding loans, Corning 
15 
is obligated to make regular repayments of 
16 
principal to its lenders.  Since depreciation 
17 
and deferred taxes are being fully used to fund 
18 
capital expenditures, those sources of cash are 
19 
not available for repaying principal.  Instead, 
20 
its principal repayments will have to be funded 
21 
by raising new capital or an increase in 
22 
retained earnings.  Most likely these funds 
23 
would be raised through new borrowing.  The 
24 
1128


--- Page 1129 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
19 
Company did not consider this when estimating 
1 
how much new debt it would borrow. 
2 
Q. 
Please explain the Company’s assumption that new
3 
capital will be raised on a 60%/40% debt/equity 
4 
basis, and why it is problematic. 
5 
A. 
Corning’s forecasted balance of debt reflects
6 
its assumption that the Company’s capital 
7 
expenditures will be funded 60% with new long-
8 
term debt and 40% with common equity.  As 
9 
Corning is not targeting a common equity ratio 
10 
of 40%, this assumption is unreasonable.  
11 
Corning’s equity ratio was 48.04% as of

Q. 
The Panel mentioned earlier that it recommended 
4 
a hypothetical capital structure of 46.00% 
5 
48.00% in part because it is difficult to

determine if Corning and Holdings were employing 
7 
rational financing policies.  Please explain the 
8 
significance of rational financing policies. 
9 
A. 
Nearly all utility holding companies have both 
10 
regulated utility assets, as well as unregulated 
11 
businesses.  Given the significant differences 
12 
in business risk between the unregulated 
13 
operations and the regulated utilities, there 
14 
should be differing amounts of equity employed 
15 
in each type of business commensurate with the 
16 
particular degree of risk.  Rational financing 
17 
policies would ensure that the higher business 
18 
risk activities of a diversified entity are 
19 
offset by the deployment of lower risk financial 
20 
practices than would be needed to finance its 
21 
lower business risk segments.   
22 
Q. 
Please explain, in general, the concept of 
23 
business risk and financial risk. 
24 
1138


--- Page 1139 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
29 
A. 
Business risk is the risk inherent in a
1 
company’s operation and reflects the risk that 
2 
it will fail to achieve its expected financial 
3 
performance.  It is affected by factors such as 
4 
a company’s sensitivity to the overall economy, 
5 
the level of competition it faces, and the 
6 
diversity of its customer and/or supplier bases.  
7 
Financial risk, on the other hand, is the risk a 
8 
company faces due to the amount of leverage 
9 
employed to finance its capital investments.  
10 
Generally speaking, regulated utilities and 
11 
holding companies that are heavily utility-
12 
focused tend to have low levels of business risk 
13 
compared to companies in other industries. 
14 
Q. 
Given the typical variances in business risk
15 
between utilities and non-utility companies, 
16 
what capitalization differences would be 
17 
expected between utility subsidiaries and non-
18 
utility subsidiaries? 
19 
A. 
As a result of their low business risk nature,
20 
utility companies are generally able to employ 
21 
significantly higher levels of financial risk 
22 
than their non-utility counterparts and still be 
23 
considered creditworthy.  Because unregulated 
24 
1139


--- Page 1140 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
30 
 
businesses are riskier than utilities, as they 
1 
face competition and do not benefit from set 
2 
rates designed to recover all of their prudent 
3 
costs, such businesses would be expected to 
4 
have, relative to utilities, larger equity 
5 
“cushions” to protect against variances in 
6 
earnings impacting their ability to meet debt 
7 
obligations.  Essentially, this means that non-
8 
utility businesses typically need to maintain 
9 
lower levels of financial leverage than 
10 
regulated utilities in order to be seen as a 
11 
worthwhile credit risk to a potential lender. 
12

A. 
The reason we recommend the use of a no-change 
8 
forecast is because movements in long-term 
9 
Treasury yields are difficult to predict.  Other 
10 
forecasts are not only poor predictors of the 
11 
magnitude of the expected change in Treasury 
12 
yields, but they are also not reliable regarding 
13 
the direction of the change.  Instead, the best 
14 
estimate of future long-term interest rates is a 
15 
no-change forecast, also known as a “random-
16 
walk” forecast.  In other words, the current 
17 
yields of these debt instruments should be 
18 
employed as an estimate of future interest 
19 
rates, as that is the most accurate forecast. 
20 
Q.  Does the Panel have any support for using a no-
21 
change forecast to estimate future Treasury 
22 
yields? 
23 
A. 
Yes.  This is discussed in a study entitled, “On 
24 
1148

39

SUMMARY OF ROE RECOMMENDATION 
5 
Q. 
What methodology did the Panel use to determine
6 
its recommended ROE for Corning? 
7 
A. 
Using a DCF analysis, weighted two-thirds, and
8 
the average of two CAPM analyses, weighted one-
9 
third, we estimated the cost of equity for a 
10 
proxy group consisting of 28 electric utility 
11 
holding companies plus five natural gas utility 
12 
holding companies which resulted in our 
13 
recommendation of 8.45%.  
14 
Q. 
Please explain why the Panel specifically
15 
recommends that the DCF methodology be given a 
16 
two-thirds weighting and the CAPM result one 
17 
third weighting? 
18 
A. 
Over the past 20 years, Staff has advocated that
19 
the CAPM be weighted less than the DCF in the 
20 
overall ROE calculation.  During this time, 
21 
Staff testimony addressing ROE has consistently 
22 
noted the numerous reasons why the DCF has been 
23 
and should continue to be, the preferred 
24 
1156


--- Page 1157 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
47 
 
methodology. 
1 
 
 
Estimating the cost of equity requires 
2 
using methodologies that are not perfect.  Of 
3 
all the approaches available, however, the DCF 
4 
and the CAPM are by far the least flawed and, 
5 
between the two, the DCF is superior.  In fact, 
6 
the Commission has noted the relative strengths 
7 
of the DCF methodology in many of its previous 
8 
rate orders.  For example, on page 14 of the 
9 
Rate Order issued October 18, 2007 in Case 06-E-
10 
1433, Orange and Rockland Utilities, Inc., the 
11 
Commission stated that “the method offers the 
12 
significant benefit of reliance on readily 
13 
available, objective data to measure an 
14 
indicator of real importance to investors.”

USE OF PROXY GROUP 
16 
Q. 
Why is a proxy group used to estimate Corning’s 
17 
cost of equity? 
18 
A. 
The use of a proxy group to determine the cost 
19 
of equity is necessary for several reasons. 
20 
First, the Company’s common stock is not 
21 
publicly traded, and, thus, direct DCF and CAPM 
22 
analyses of the Company are not possible. 
23 
Equally important is that DCF analyses for 
24 
1157


--- Page 1158 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
48 
individual companies rely on equity analysts’ 
1 
estimates of growth, and those estimates, by 
2 
their nature, could be biased or potentially 
3 
inaccurate.  Similarly, beta determinations used 
4 
in the CAPM methodology are based on historical 
5 
observations that, due to circumstances such as 
6 
corporate restructurings or industry 
7 
transformations, may not be representative of 
8 
the level of earnings volatility expected in the 
9 
future.  By employing a sufficiently large proxy 
10 
group of similarly situated companies in our 
11 
analyses, however, we can minimize the 
12 
undesirable effects of bias, both upward and 
13 
downward, or inaccurate estimates for any one 
14 
company. 
15 
Even if one wanted to conduct DCF and CAPM 
16 
analyses on Holdings, as Corning’s publicly 
17 
traded parent company, rather than a proxy 
18 
group, this would be highly problematic.  That 
19 
is because the common stock of Holdings is very 
20 
thinly traded.  Often sales of stocks that are 
21 
thinly traded will cause market prices to change 
22 
abruptly, especially if a large block of shares 
23 
is sold at once.  When such a sale occurs, the 
24 
1158


--- Page 1159 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
49 
 
sale price may be far removed from the stock’s 
1 
true value.  Therefore, at any point in time, 
2 
the sale price may not match the true value of 
3 
the stock, and a direct cost of equity analysis 
4 
would not yield accurate results. 
5 
Q. 
What are the most important considerations for 
6 
selecting a proxy group? 
7 
A. 
First, it is important to determine the specific 
8 
industry classification of the subject company 
9 
to identify its true peers.  Second, once the 
10 
appropriate group of peer companies is 
11 
established, careful consideration must be given 
12 
to determining the appropriate screening 
13 
criteria to establish a group of companies that 
14 
is both sufficiently large and of similar risk 
15 
to the company in question.  A careful balance 
16 
must be struck between these two potentially 
17 
conflicting goals.  While the objective is to 
18 
select a group of companies whose risks closely 
19 
match those of the subject company, it is also 
20 
important that the proxy group be large enough 
21 
to provide sufficient confidence in the results.  
22 
The greater the number of suitable companies 
23 
that can be found, the less sensitive the 
24 
1159


--- Page 1160 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
50 
 
overall cost of equity estimate will be to the 
1 
fluctuations or irregularities in the data 
2 
related to any one particular company.

DISCOUNTED CASH FLOW (DCF) METHODOLOGY  
15 
Q.  Please explain the basic theory underlying the 
16 
DCF methodology. 
17 
A.  The DCF approach can be applied to any 
18 
investment instrument that has an intrinsic 
19 
value.  The DCF approach, as it relates to 
20 
common stock, recognizes that companies create 
21 
value for their stockholders by using their 
22 
earnings in a number of ways, the most important 
23 
of which, by far, is through the payment of cash 
24 
1166


--- Page 1167 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
57 
 
dividends.  Alternatively, earnings that are 
1 
retained by companies can be used to create 
2 
value by investing in capital projects designed 
3 
to increase future profits.  The retained 
4 
earnings can also create value by retiring debt, 
5 
which reduces interest expense, thereby 
6 
resulting in greater cash flow available to 
7 
stockholders, and by buying back some of the 
8 
Company’s common stock, which increases future 
9 
earnings on a per-share basis. 
10 
Q. 
What principles support the DCF? 
11 
A. 
It is important to note that, while earnings 
12 
drive companies’ dividend payout policies, the 
13 
value of the companies’ common stock is equal to 
14 
the present value of all future dividends.  This 
15 
is because the earnings that are retained will 
16 
only have value to the stockholder when they are 
17 
paid as dividends in the future.  Underlying 
18 
this principle is the strong assumption in 
19 
capital market theory that companies earn the 
20 
same return on retained earnings as the market 
21 
demands on their common stock.  Also fundamental 
22 
to the DCF methodology is the sentiment that 
23 
cash and/or earnings held in the future do not 
24 
1167


--- Page 1168 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
58 
hold the same worth as cash or earnings held in 
1 
the present.  Due to the time preference of 
2 
people to spend their cash today rather than 
3 
waiting for the effects of inflation and 
4 
productivity to impact future cash flows, the 
5 
DCF discounts the future expected cash flows 
6 
according to investors’ return requirements. 
7 
Q. 
Why does the Panel place primary reliance on the
8 
results of the DCF methodology? 
9 
A. 
The main reason the DCF methodology continues to
10 
be the preferred approach for determining a 
11 
company’s cost of equity is that investors’ 
12 
immediate return requirements, as observed in 
13 
current stock prices and recent dividends, are 
14 
readily quantifiable.  The other principle 
15 
methodology, the CAPM, only relies tangentially, 
16 
through the use of utility beta values, upon 
17 
direct observations of actual utility investor 
18 
behavior.  The primary challenge in applying the 
19 
DCF is determining the rate of growth in future 
20 
dividends that investors expect. 
21 
Given the relatively mature and stable 
22 
nature of the utility industry, such estimates 
23 
can be derived with a reasonable degree of 
24 
1168


--- Page 1169 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
59 
certitude.  Also, rational utility investors 
1 
expect the growth in future dividends to 
2 
generally track the changes in output, or growth 
3 
in the overall economy, as measured by growth in 
4 
the nominal Gross Domestic Product (GDP). 
5 
Moreover, just as nominal GDP growth 
6 
incorporates gains achieved through the 
7 
application of new technologies, otherwise known 
8 
as productivity, and the effects of changes in 
9 
price levels, the investors’ growth 
10 
expectations, too, will reflect assumptions 
11 
regarding productivity and the rate of 
12 
inflation.  Consequently, when practiced with 
13 
the application of well-reasoned growth rate 
14 
estimates, such as those used in our approach, 
15 
the intuitiveness of the DCF methodology is 
16 
abundantly clear. 
17 
This intuitiveness is a primary reason that 
18 
the Commission has regularly found this 
19 
methodology to be the best tool for estimating 
20 
the cost of equity for a regulated utility.  In 
21 
the Rate Order issued April 24, 2009 in Case 08-
22 
E-0539, Consolidated Edison Company of New York,
23 
Inc., the Commission stated that a reason it
24 
1169


--- Page 1170 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
60 
 
accords a two-thirds weighting to the DCF 
1 
methodology is that “…the DCF relies on readily 
2 
available data to make objective estimates of 
3 
investors’ return requirements.  While the DCF 
4 
has one input of primary controversy (growth), 
5 
two CAPM inputs (beta and the market risk 
6 
premium) are dependent on estimates which are 
7 
contested and volatile.” 
8 
Q. 
Please describe the Panel’s DCF methodology and 
9 
its result. 
10 
A. 
Our DCF model is a two-stage “dividend discount” 
11 
model that is consistent with the financial 
12 
theory that the value of a company’s stock is 
13 
equivalent to its future cash flows.  Our 
14 
dividend discount model forecasts those cash 
15 
flows into the future and discounts them 
16 
 
back to their present value.  It also explicitly 
17 
recognizes that a company’s short-term growth 
18 
expectations do not necessarily equal long-term 
19 
expectations.  The first stage uses analysts’ 
20 
near-term estimates to derive the short-term 
21 
growth rate, while the second stage is based on 
22 
a calculation of a sustainable growth rate.  Our 
23 
DCF calculation for the proxy group is shown on 
24 
1170


--- Page 1171 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
61 
pages one and two of Exhibit__(FP-6). 
1 
Q. 
How did the Panel calculate the stock prices
2 
that were used in its DCF model? 
3 
A. 
We used the average of the high and low price
4 
for each month during the three-month period 
5 
ending May 2020. 
6 
Q. 
How are dividends projected to change over time?
7 
A. 
Our analysis maintains the same approach that
8 
Staff has relied on for many years.  In the 
9 
first stage of our DCF model, for the years 2020 
10 
through 2024, we rely on Value Line’s forecasted 
11 
dividends for each company in the proxy group.  
12 
In the second stage, for the years 2025 and 
13 
beyond, a sustainable growth rate is calculated 
14 
for each company within the proxy group.  This 
15 
long-term growth rate is primarily based on each 
16 
company’s expected earned return on average 
17 
common equity and its projected retention of 
18 
earnings.  Our sustainable growth rate also 
19 
incorporates growth resulting from an increase 
20 
in common share balances over time.  We believe 
21 
that using analyst forecasts for dividend growth 
22 
in the near term is reasonable, but analysts 
23 
generally do not publish dividend forecasts for 
24 
1171

longer than a few years into the future.  So, 
1 
unless one makes the unreasonable assumption

that near-term estimates of growth will continue

impossible to employ dividend growth forecasts

by solving for the discount rate necessary to

dividend stream for each company equal to its

current stock price.

18 
its financial leverage.

21 
CAPITAL ASSET PRICING MODEL 
22 
Q. 
Please describe the basic theory underlying the
23 
CAPM. 
24 
1176


--- Page 1177 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
67 
A. 
The principle behind the CAPM theory is that
1 
there is no premium, in terms of expected 
2 
return, for bearing risks that can be eliminated 
3 
through diversification.  According to the CAPM, 
4 
rational investors will hold a portfolio of 
5 
stocks (generally 60 or more) such that the 
6 
overall risk of that portfolio, in terms of the 
7 
variability of its returns, closely approximates 
8 
that of the market as a whole.  Thus, the only 
9 
risk that matters in the CAPM equation is said 
10 
to be “systematic” risk or risk that cannot be 
11 
diversified away. 
12 
Systematic risk is a risk common to all 
13 
equity securities that cannot be eliminated 
14 
through diversification.  It is measured by a 
15 
variable denominated as “beta.”  Systematic risk 
16 
is also known as market risk, which is the 
17 
uncertainty inherent in the entire market or 
18 
market segment.  Changes in interest rates, 
19 
recessions, wars, and pandemics are all examples 
20 
of systematic risks. 
21 
On the other hand, “unsystematic” risk is 
22 
risk that is specific to a particular stock.  
23 
While it is assumed that most stocks tend to go 
24 
1177


--- Page 1178 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
68 
 
along with the general market, at least to some 
1 
extent, factors that are specific to an 
2 
individual stock are said to affect its 
3 
“unsystematic” risk. 
4 
 
 
According to the CAPM, the appropriate way 
5 
to measure an individual stock’s risk is through 
6 
a correlation of its return relative to the 
7 
market as a whole, known as beta.  A stock with 
8 
a beta of 1.0 has a return that mirrors the 
9 
return of the “market,” usually taken to mean 
10 
the S&P 500, as a whole.  Betas of less than 
11 
1.0, which are typical for utility stocks given 
12 
the moderating influence of regulation and the 
13 
accompanying perception of reduced risk, 
14 
indicate that the stocks are less volatile than 
15 
the market as a whole.  The CAPM informs us that 
16 
investors will only be compensated for their 
17 
actual risk, as measured by beta.  Thus, in the 
18 
case of estimating the return requirements of 
19 
utility investors, the CAPM result will reflect 
20 
the degree to which utility stocks are less 
21 
volatile than the market as a whole. 
22 
Q. 
On what assumptions is the CAPM based? 
23 
A. 
The model is based on the assumptions that: (1) 
24 
1178


--- Page 1179 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
69 
 
the capital market is competitive and efficient; 
1 
(2) investors are risk-averse and demand higher 
2 
returns for higher risk; (3) market participants 
3 
can lend and borrow unlimited amounts under the 
4 
risk-free rate of interest; and (4) investors 
5 
hold diversified portfolios and operate in 
6 
capital markets with no transaction costs, 
7 
taxes, or restrictions on financial 
8 
transactions.  Under the CAPM model, the 
9 
expected return of a security or a portfolio is 
10 
equal to the rate on a risk-free security plus a 
11 
risk premium multiplied by the asset’s 
12 
systematic risk.   
13 
Q. 
Please describe the methodology the Panel used 
14 
to determine its CAPM results. 
15 
A. 
Consistent with the approach that Staff has 
16 
employed and that the Commission has adopted for 
17 
many years, we averaged the results of two forms 
18 
of the CAPM: the Traditional CAPM and the Zero 
19 
Beta CAPM. 
20 
Q. 
Why did the Panel use two forms of the CAPM? 
21 
A. 
Research has indicated that the Traditional CAPM 
22 
model may underestimate the required return when 
23 
betas are below 1.0.  Therefore, in an effort to 
24 
1179


--- Page 1180 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
70 
avoid an underestimated return, we use a Zero 
1 
Beta methodology as well.  By averaging in the 
2 
result of the Zero Beta approach, which is only 
3 
partially determined by the beta used, this 
4 
tendency is addressed and corrected for, and 
5 
ultimately enhances the accuracy of our overall 
6 
CAPM ROE determination.  
7 
Q. 
Please describe the calculation used in the
8 
Traditional CAPM. 
9 
A. 
The Traditional CAPM formula is:
10 
K = Rf + β*(Rm-Rf), where: 
11 
K = investor’s required return or equity cost of 
12 
capital; 
13 
Rf = risk-free rate; 
14 
β = beta; and 
15 
Rm = market rate of return.  
16 
We note that the term Rm–Rf is commonly known as 
17 
the market risk premium (MRP). 
18 
Q.  Please describe the calculation used in the Zero
19 
Beta CAPM method. 
20 
A. 
We used the same inputs as in the Traditional
21 
CAPM methodology; however, instead of 
22 
multiplying beta by the MRP, as shown in the 
23 
calculation of the Traditional CAPM methodology,  
24 
1180


--- Page 1181 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
71 
 
we determined the MRP for the proxy group by 
1 
multiplying 0.75 by beta by the MRP and adding  
2 
0.25 times the MRP.  This can be expressed as:   
3 
 
K = Rf + 0.75*β*(Rm-Rf) + 0.25*(Rm-Rf). 
4 
Q. 
How does a company’s beta measure risk? 
5 
A. 
Beta is a measure of how closely correlated the 
6 
return for a particular stock is to the return 
7 
on the market as a whole.  A beta of 1.0 
8 
indicates that the stock’s return mirrors the 
9 
return of the market as a whole.  Betas of less 
10 
than 1.0, which are typical for utility stocks, 
11 
indicate that the stocks are less volatile than 
12 
the market as a whole.  Accordingly, the CAPM 
13 
informs investors that they will be compensated 
14 
only for actual risk, as measured by beta.  
15 
Thus, in terms of estimating the return 
16 
requirements of utility investors, the CAPM 
17 
results will reflect the degree to which utility 
18 
stocks are less volatile relative to the general 
19 
market. 
20

Q. 
Please explain how the calculation of the beta
16 
can be problematic. 
17 
A. 
First, beta is supposed to represent the future
18 
volatility of a given stock relative to the 
19 
market as a whole.  However, because future 
20 
volatility is an unknown, betas must be measured 
21 
on a historical basis.  The problem with using 
22 
historically derived betas, though, is that when 
23 
the systematic risks of a firm or industry 
24 
1185


--- Page 1186 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
76 
change, these historically derived betas may not 
1 
be reliable indicators of future volatility.  
2 
Thus, the measurement of past stock price 
3 
movements is a poor predictor of future stock 
4 
price changes.   
5 
Another, and perhaps more significant, 
6 
shortcoming of beta calculations is the often 
7 
wide disparity of betas between the various 
8 
firms that report this measure.  For instance, 
9 
Staff has exclusively relied on betas reported 
10 
by Value Line for at least the past twenty 
11 
years, as they are generally calculated over a 
12 
five-year period.  This is long enough to 
13 
produce reliable estimates but recent enough to 
14 
reflect current market conditions.  Some firms 
15 
use either much shorter or much longer time 
16 
periods in their calculations of beta.  We find 
17 
that the five-year time period used by Value 
18 
Line produces reliable estimates of volatility.  
19 
Moreover, Value Line also “smoothes” the “raw” 
20 
betas to reflect the theory that betas have a 
21 
natural tendency to converge to 1.0.  Other 
22 
firms do not adjust the “raw” betas as Value 
23 
Line does.  Our concern is that, depending upon 
24 
1186

the source, betas can vary significantly, and 
1 
thus produce CAPM-based ROE results that differ

quite substantially solely because of the source

chosen for the beta input.

Q. 
How did the Panel determine its appropriate cost 
5 
of market return to use in its CAPM analyses, 
6 
and what were the results? 
7 
A. 
Because the cost of equity is, by its nature, a 
8 
forward-looking concept, we employed ex-ante 
9 
(forecasted) analysis, relying upon the market 
10 
return estimates for the S&P 500, as published 
11 
by Bank of America Merrill Lynch (BAML) in its 
12 
Quantitative Profile reports.  Our market rate 
13 
of return is derived from the two forward-
14 
looking returns on the market, a required return 
15 
and an implied return, as published by BAML.  
16 
Specifically, we used the monthly editions of 
17 
the Quantitative Profile reports for March 2020, 
18 
April 2020, and May 2020, and averaged the 
19 
required and implied market returns of each of 
20 
the three point-in-time forecasts, to arrive at 
21 
an appropriate market return of 10.73%.  
22 
Excerpts of these publications are included as 
23 
Exhibit__(FP-11), and the full reports can be 
24

78 
 
made available upon request.   
1 
Q. 
Why is the Panel using an average of the most 
2 
recent three months of BAML’s expected market 
3 
returns in its calculation? 
4 
A. 
Generally speaking, we use expected market 
5 
return estimates from the most recent three 
6 
months to be consistent with the timeframes of 
7 
the other data inputs used in our CAPM and DCF 
8 
calculations.  By matching the timeframe upon 
9 
which our other parameters are calculated, we 
10 
arrive at the most appropriate estimate of the 
11 
required market rate of return to use.  It is 
12 
also critical that the timeframes used to 
13 
determine the risk-free rate of return and the 
14 
market rate of return be the same in order to 
15 
validly calculate the MRP. 
16 
Q. 
How did the Panel determine the appropriate MRP 
17 
to use in its analysis? 
18 
A. 
As previously discussed, the MRP is the 
19 
difference between the expected market return on 
20 
the equity market and the return required on a 
21 
risk-free investment.  Subtracting our 1.05% 
22 
risk-free rate from the 10.73% cost of market 
23 
return yields our MRP estimate of 9.68%.

Q. 
What are some of the difficulties associated
1 
with the CAPM? 
2 
A. 
The market rate of return (Rm) includes capital
3 
gains and dividends added together.  However, 
4 
from time to time, the actual market return can 
5 
become negative due to many factors, including 
6 
recessions, war, and/or depressed earnings.  
7 
COVID-19 is an example of precisely this kind of 
8 
event risk.  Therefore, while investors expect 
9 
the market return to be positive over the long-
10 
run, they also expect the market return to 
11 
fluctuate in the short-term, punctuated by 
12 
periods of negative return.  Thus, it is 
13 
important that the application of an expected 
14 
long-term market return consider realistic 
15 
growth rates and current economic factors.   
16

6 
Q. 
Please describe the Panel’s core concerns about
7 
Concentric’s DCF models. 
8 
A. 
We are concerned about Concentric’s application
9 
of 1) earnings growth rates rather than dividend 
10 
growth rates for the short-term; 2) an excessive 
11 
long-term growth rate; and, 3) the assumed 
12

13 
Q. 
Please explain why Concentric’s use of earnings
14 
rather than dividends to estimate the short-term 
15 
growth rates in its DCF model is problematic. 
16 
A. 
Concentric’s DCF model uses earnings growth rate
17 
forecasts published by analysts in order to 
18 
estimate short-term growth in dividends.  This 
19 
approach assumes that growth in dividends will 
20 
approximate growth in earnings, although 
21 
Concentric did not provide any evidence 
22 
demonstrating that this assumption is valid.  
23 
Concentric’s assumption is unproven and 
24 
1212


--- Page 1213 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
103 
 
unnecessary, given that dividend growth rates or 
1 
forecasts are readily available.  This approach 
2 
also stands in direct contrast to the basic 
3 
premise of the DCF, which measures the present 
4 
value of future dividends, not earnings. 
5 
Q.  On page 56 of Concentric’s testimony, it states 
6 
that “earnings are the fundamental driver of a 
7 
company’s ability to pay dividends, therefore, 
8 
earnings growth is the appropriate measure of a 
9 
company’s long-term growth.”  How can 
10 
Concentric’s use of earnings growth instead of 
11 
dividend growth lead to inaccuracy in its DCF 
12 
model? 
13 
A.  Concentric's use of earnings growth in its DCF 
14 
model fails to properly account for the division 
15 
of annual earnings into retained earnings and 
16 
dividends.  Investors recognize that annual 
17 
earnings represent a company's profit before the 
18 
consideration of its dividend payout and the use 
19 
of retained earnings.  Retained earnings provide 
20 
a company’s management with the flexibility to 
21 
maintain its current dividends should it suffer 
22 
a loss of revenue or unplanned expenses, 
23 
effectively providing a cushion for investors 
24 
1213


--- Page 1214 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
104 
 
when profitability shrinks.  In fact, a 
1 
company’s dividend policy is one of the ways 
2 
that it insulates shareholders from the 
3 
volatility of earnings from one time period to 
4 
the next.  Indeed, investors generally prefer 
5 
dividends to be steadily increasing and 
6 
predictably regular.  Thus, Concentric's primary 
7 
reliance on earnings growth in its DCF model 
8 
rather than dividend growth reflects neither 
9 
realistic growth rates nor typical corporate 
10 
practice. 
11 
Q. 
What additional reasons make Concentric’s 
12 
application of earnings growth, rather than 
13 
dividend growth, in its DCF model problematic?   
14 
A. 
Concentric’s DCF model assumes dividend growth 
15 
will match earnings growth.  In addition, its 
16 
model does not account for the issuance of 
17 
common equity shares in the future.  Our DCF 
18 
model is more comprehensive because it uses 
19 
actual forecasted dividend growth rates, and it 
20 
accounts for changes in the number of common 
21 
equity shares.   
22 
 
 
Furthermore, it is highly unlikely that 
23 
investors would rely exclusively on the earnings 
24 
1214


--- Page 1215 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
105 
growth rate forecasts of Wall Street analysts in 
1 
determining short-term dividend projections.  In 
2

3 
S. Harris article, “Using Analysts’ Growth
4 
Forecasts to Estimate Shareholder Required Rates
5 
of Return” as follows: “a growing body of
6 
knowledge shows that analysts’ earnings

forecasts are indeed reflected in stock prices.”
8 
We agree that a company’s stock price does
9 
indeed reflect published earnings forecasts from
10 
analysts, in so far as all relevant information
11 
is incorporated into a company’s stock price.
12 
However, forecasted earnings are far from the
13

14 
information considered by investors and
15

19 
the importance of dividends to shareholder

21 
especially concerned with the prospect of future

dividends.  Furthermore, Concentric has not
23 
provided any basis to support of a one-to-one
24 
1215


--- Page 1216 ---

linear relationship of earnings growth to 
1

3 
including individual company cash flow

7 
will not look at forecasted earnings alone in a

relevant information when considering an

6 
ratemaking treatment will need to be 
7 
reevaluated.

TRUE-UP OF INTEREST COSTS 
9 
Q. 
Please describe the true-up provision that the 
10 
Company was authorized in the 2017 Rate Order 
11 
pertaining to its interest costs. 
12 
A. 
The Joint Proposal adopted by the Commission in 
13 
Case 16-G-0369 provides that, “if the Company 
14 
procures fixed rate debt, interest costs will be 
15 
trued up to the actual interest cost of that 
16 
debt, subject to the following conditions: the 
17 
debt cost must be equivalent to the cost of BBB 
18 
rated, or above, debt; the true-up will apply to 
19 
no more than 75% of the Company’s variable rate 
20 
debt, even if the Company converts a greater 
21 
percentage; the “new” fixed rate debt must have 
22 
at least a five-year average life; and no more 
23 
than $5.0 million of such “new” debt may come 
24 
1243


--- Page 1244 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
134 
 
due in any one year.” 
1 
Q. 
Please explain the purpose of permitting a true-
2 
up of Corning’s interest rate cost in that case. 
3 
A. 
At that time, Corning’s debt portfolio consisted 
4 
entirely of variable rate debt.  The cost of 
5 
loans bearing a variable interest rate, as the 
6 
terminology implies, can vary from time to time 
7 
as the interest rate environment changes, and 
8 
the potential changes to the interest rate are 
9 
open-ended.  Therefore, the borrower bears the 
10 
risk that interest rates may change.  At the 
11 
time, Staff was encouraging Corning to eliminate 
12 
this risk by converting its variable rate debt 
13 
to fixed rate debt, which essentially transfers 
14 
interest rate risk to the lender.  As 
15 
compensation for accepting this risk, a lender 
16 
usually charges the borrower a higher initial 
17 
interest rate when agreeing to fixed interest 
18 
rate debt.  This would have been a significant 
19 
disincentive for Corning, as a borrower, to 
20 
convert its loans from a variable interest rate 
21 
to a fixed interest rate.  To alleviate this 
22 
disincentive, a true-up mechanism was instituted 
23 
to enable the Company to recover the prudently 
24 
1244


--- Page 1245 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
135 
incurred costs associated with the fixed rate 
1 
debt it procures in order to repay its variable 
2 
rate debt. 
3 
Q. 
Has the Company converted its variable rate debt
4 
to fixed rate debt since the time the Joint 
5 
Proposal was adopted? 
6 
A. 
Yes.  The Company converted its debt to a fixed
7 
interest rate on November 30, 2017.  It has 
8 
exclusively procured fixed rate debt for its 
9 
long-term borrowing ever since. 
10 
Q. 
How does the Company propose to recover the cost
11 
of associated with the fixed rate debt? 
12 
A. 
In the 2017 Rate Order, Corning was authorized
13 
rates predicated on an interest rate of 3.25%.  
14 
Only the cost of fixed rate debt in excess of 
15 
this amount has not yet been recovered in rates.  
16 
Corning proposes that the excess interest costs 
17 
be booked as a deferred debit and amortized over 
18 
36 months beginning February 1, 2021. 
19 
Q. 
Does the Panel agree with this method of
20 
recovery? 
21 
A. 
Yes.  We have no objection to recovering these
22 
costs through a deferral mechanism.  However, 
23 
Staff recommends an amortization period of 60 
24 
1245


--- Page 1246 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
136 
 
months rather than 36. 
1 
Q. 
How much in fixed rate interest costs does the 
2 
Company propose to collect? 
3 
A. 
$804,222. 
4 
Q. 
Does the Panel agree with this amount? 
5 
A. 
No, we do not. 
6 
Q. 
Please explain. 
7 
A. 
Based on our calculations, we find that the 
8 
Company is entitled to recover $597,803 for this 
9 
purpose. 
10 
Q. 
How did the Panel calculate this amount? 
11 
A. 
We began by determining the maximum amount of 
12 
debt that was eligible to be trued up.  As noted 
13 
earlier in our testimony, the true-up applies to 
14 
no more than 75% of the Company’s variable rate 
15 
debt.  According capitalization matrix in the 
16 
2017 Rate Order, Appendix L of the Joint 
17 
Proposal, Corning’s rates were predicated on a 
18 
balance of debt that was slightly less than 
19 
$28.0 million, and 75% of this would be just 
20 
under $21.0 million.  Corning has borrowed more 
21 
fixed rate debt than this, so the amount of debt 
22 
eligible for true-up is capped at $21.0 million.  
23 
Next, because the Joint Proposal prescribes a 
24 
1246


--- Page 1247 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
137 
 
true-up to the Company’s actual interest cost, 
1 
we calculated the actual embedded cost of its 
2 
fixed rate long-term debt for each month it was 
3 
operating under the current rate plan.  This 
4 
varied between 4.00% and 4.25% per annum from 
5 
month to month.  Multiplying $21.0 million by 
6 
the actual cost of debt in each month equals how 
7 
much the Company was entitled to collect in 
8 
interest costs.  From this, we subtracted the 
9 
amount that Corning was authorized to collect in 
10 
rates, which in each month was equal to $21.0 
11 
million multiplied by the authorized interest 
12 
rate of 3.25% and divided by 12.  The difference 
13 
represents what Corning was permitted to defer 
14 
for future recovery in each month.  The sum 
15 
total of the monthly deferrals is equal to 
16 
$597,803.  A schedule demonstrating our 
17 
calculations is included as Exhibit__(FP-18).

19

1247

4 
Q. 
What are the RRA rankings, and what do they
5 
indicate? 
6 
A. 
RRA evaluates the regulatory climates of utility
7 
companies operating in the United States on an 
8 
ongoing basis.  Numerous factors affecting each 
9 
state’s regulatory environment are measured by 
10 
RRA in its evaluation process.  RRA has three 
11 
principal rating categories of “Above Average”, 
12 
“Average” and “Below Average”.  Within each of 
13 
those categories, the numbers “1”, “2”, and “3” 
14 
indicate relative position, with “1” being the 
15 
strongest.  In total, RRA has nine rating 
16 
categories ranging from the highest and most 
17 
constructive climate of “Above Average/1” to the 
18 
lowest and least-constructive climate of “Below 
19 
Average/3”.  New York’s “Average/1” rating by 
20 
RRA indicates it is 1 notch stronger than the 
21 
“Average/2” rating that Concentric found to be 
22 
typical of the Combined Proxy Group.

24 
1248


--- Page 1249 ---
Case 20-G-0101 FINANCE PANEL 
 
 
139 
 
analysis of the RRA regulatory rankings? 
1 
A. 
Concentric failed to accurately reflect the 
2 
overall regulatory ratings of companies in its 
3 
proxy groups.  Its RRA analysis is based on the 
4 
regulated subsidiaries of the companies in its 
5 
proxy groups, but it does not consider the 
6

7

8

9 
relative impact of each subsidiary on the 
10 
parents’ overall level of regulatory support.  
11 
For example, Concentric gave an equal weighting 
12 
to Consolidated Edison, Inc.’s two regulatory 
13 
jurisdictions, New York and New Jersey, even 
14 
though the New York operations account for 
15 
nearly 95% of Consolidated Edison, Inc.’s total 
16 
regulated assets.  Thus, Concentric’s simplistic 
17 
analysis does not reflect the actual regulatory 
18 
risk faced by the companies in its proxy group.
